questions.title: INNER JOIN vs. LEFT JOIN
questions.prompt: In SQL Server, what is the difference between an INNER JOIN and a LEFT JOIN? Specifically, what happens to rows that don't have a match on the other side in each case?
questions.modelAnswer: INNER JOIN returns only the rows where the ON condition evaluates true on both sides — any row from either table that has no match on the other side is dropped from the result entirely. LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the table named in the FROM clause (the 'left' table), whether or not it has a match in the table named after JOIN (the 'right' table). When a left-table row has no match, every column that would have come from the right table comes back as NULL instead of the row being dropped. 'Left' and 'right' describe position in the query text — the table in FROM is left, the table after JOIN is right — not anything about the size or importance of the data. A common real use of LEFT JOIN is combining it with WHERE <right-table-column> IS NULL to find rows that have no match at all, since that column can only be NULL if the join failed to find a partner row.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it with a concrete example: if I join Product to SalesOrderDetail with an INNER JOIN, I only see products that have actually sold — a product sitting in inventory with zero orders just disappears from the result, because there's nothing on the right side to pair it with. If my actual question is 'show me every product, including the ones that have never sold,' INNER JOIN can't answer that by definition, so I switch to a LEFT JOIN from Product. Now every product shows up, and for the ones with no matching order, the order columns just come back NULL. That NULL is actually useful — if I add WHERE OrderQty IS NULL to that LEFT JOIN, I've just built a 'products that have never sold' report, which is a query I get asked for constantly in a reporting role. The one thing I'm careful to remember is that left and right only refer to where I physically wrote the table in the query, not which table is 'bigger' or more important.
questions.example:
-- INNER JOIN: only products with at least one order line
SELECT p.Name, p.ListPrice, sod.OrderQty
FROM Production.Product AS p
INNER JOIN Sales.SalesOrderDetail AS sod
    ON p.ProductID = sod.ProductID;

-- LEFT JOIN: every product, NULL-filled when there's no match
SELECT p.Name, p.ListPrice, sod.OrderQty
FROM Production.Product AS p
LEFT JOIN Sales.SalesOrderDetail AS sod
    ON p.ProductID = sod.ProductID;

-- Finding products that have NEVER sold
SELECT p.Name
FROM Production.Product AS p
LEFT JOIN Sales.SalesOrderDetail AS sod
    ON p.ProductID = sod.ProductID
WHERE sod.ProductID IS NULL;
commonMistakes: Thinking 'left' and 'right' describe which table has more rows or matters more, instead of just position in the FROM/JOIN clause
Forgetting that unmatched right-side columns come back as NULL, then getting confused when COUNT() or SUM() on those columns behaves unexpectedly
Using INNER JOIN when the real goal is to find rows with no match — that specifically requires LEFT JOIN plus an IS NULL check
Not realizing WHERE runs after the join, so a WHERE clause on a right-side column can accidentally turn a LEFT JOIN back into something that behaves like an INNER JOIN
keyPoints: INNER JOIN returns only rows matching on both sides
LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the table named in FROM, matched or not
Left/right refer to position in the query, not data meaning or size
Unmatched right-side columns come back as NULL in a LEFT JOIN
LEFT JOIN + IS NULL is the standard pattern for finding unmatched rows

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what each join type returns
Explains NULL behavior for unmatched LEFT JOIN rows
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: Primary keys vs. foreign keys
questions.prompt: What does a PRIMARY KEY constraint guarantee about a column, and what does a FOREIGN KEY constraint enforce between two tables? What happens if you try to insert a row that violates a foreign key?
questions.modelAnswer: A primary key guarantees two things at once about a column (or set of columns): every value is unique, and no value is ever NULL — together that means a primary key value always identifies exactly one row. Creating a primary key without specifying otherwise also builds a clustered index on it by default, physically sorting the table by that key. A foreign key enforces referential integrity: every value in the foreign-key column must already exist as a primary-key value in the referenced table. Trying to insert or update a row with a foreign-key value that doesn't exist in the referenced table fails with error 547 — the database physically refuses to create the orphaned row. ON DELETE CASCADE changes the default behavior (which blocks deleting a referenced row while dependents still point to it) so that deleting a parent row automatically deletes its dependent rows too.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe the primary key as the table's identity guarantee — Production.Product's primary key, ProductID, means I can always find exactly one product for a given ID, never zero, never two. The foreign key is what makes a JOIN trustworthy: Product.ProductSubcategoryID is a foreign key to ProductSubcategory, so SQL Server physically won't let me insert a product pointing at a subcategory that doesn't exist. If I try, I get error 547, which is the database doing its job, not a bug to work around. I'm careful with ON DELETE CASCADE, though — it's convenient for cleaning up dependent rows automatically, but on a deep relationship chain it can silently delete far more data than I expect, so I think through the blast radius before turning it on.
commonMistakes: Thinking a primary key only guarantees uniqueness and forgetting it also guarantees NOT NULL
Not realizing a primary key builds a clustered index by default unless you explicitly say NONCLUSTERED
Assuming a foreign key violation is just a warning rather than a hard failure (error 547) that blocks the write
Adding ON DELETE CASCADE without considering how far the deletion could cascade through a longer relationship chain
keyPoints: Primary key = unique + NOT NULL, identifying exactly one row
Primary key creates a clustered index by default
Foreign key enforces that a value must exist as a primary key in another table
Violating a foreign key raises Error 547
ON DELETE CASCADE changes the default block-on-delete behavior

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes what a primary key guarantees
Correctly describes referential integrity and Error 547
Mentions the clustered index / cascade nuance

questions.title: UNION vs. UNION ALL
questions.prompt: In T-SQL, what's the difference between UNION and UNION ALL when combining the result sets of two SELECT statements, and what two conditions must both SELECT statements satisfy before you can combine them at all?
questions.modelAnswer: UNION combines the rows returned by two (or more) SELECT statements into one result set and removes any duplicate rows from that combined set, which requires SQL Server to do an implicit sort/distinct pass over the whole combined output. UNION ALL also combines the rows, but keeps every row exactly as returned, duplicates included, and skips the dedup pass entirely -- which makes it faster and cheaper to run whenever duplicates either can't occur or genuinely don't matter. Both statements being combined must return the same number of columns, and the data type in each corresponding column position must be compatible (not necessarily identical, but implicitly convertible) -- column names in the final result come from the first SELECT statement, regardless of what the second one used.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd default to UNION ALL unless I actually have a reason to expect duplicates and need them removed, because UNION ALL skips the sort/distinct work UNION does under the hood, so it's just cheaper to run on anything beyond a trivial row count. The two things I always check before combining two SELECTs this way: same number of columns on both sides, and compatible data types lining up column-by-column -- if the second SELECT's third column is a different, incompatible type from the first's third column, the combine fails outright. One detail that trips people up is that the final column names come entirely from the first SELECT -- aliasing a column differently in the second query doesn't change anything in the output.
questions.example:
-- UNION: removes duplicate rows across both queries
SELECT FirstName, LastName FROM Person.Person WHERE LastName = 'Smith'
UNION
SELECT FirstName, LastName FROM HumanResources.Employee e
JOIN Person.Person p ON p.BusinessEntityID = e.BusinessEntityID WHERE LastName = 'Smith';

-- UNION ALL: keeps every row, including duplicates, and skips the dedup work
SELECT FirstName, LastName FROM Person.Person WHERE LastName = 'Smith'
UNION ALL
SELECT FirstName, LastName FROM HumanResources.Employee e
JOIN Person.Person p ON p.BusinessEntityID = e.BusinessEntityID WHERE LastName = 'Smith';
commonMistakes: Using UNION by default everywhere, paying for a dedup pass that isn't actually needed
Assuming the two SELECTs need identical column names instead of just a matching column count and compatible types
Not realizing the final result's column names come from the first SELECT, regardless of aliases used in the second
Forgetting ORDER BY can only appear once, at the very end of the combined statement, not after each individual SELECT
keyPoints: UNION removes duplicate rows across the combined result sets; UNION ALL keeps every row
UNION ALL is cheaper -- it skips the sort/distinct pass UNION performs
Both SELECTs must return the same number of columns with compatible data types per position
Result column names come from the first SELECT statement

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the duplicate-removal difference
Correctly states the column-count/data-type compatibility requirement
Mentions the performance implication of the dedup pass

questions.title: Spark transformations vs. actions
questions.prompt: In Spark, what's the difference between a transformation (like filter or select) and an action (like count or show), and why does Spark wait to actually run anything until an action is called?
questions.modelAnswer: A transformation (filter, select, withColumn, join, and similar) doesn't touch any data when it's called -- it just adds one more step to a logical plan Spark is building up in the background, describing what should eventually happen. An action (count, show, collect, write, and similar) is what actually triggers Spark to execute that whole accumulated plan against the real data and produce a concrete result. This is called lazy evaluation: Spark deliberately waits because it's more efficient to look at the entire chain of transformations at once and optimize it as a whole -- reordering filters, combining steps, deciding how to partition work -- than to execute each transformation immediately and separately as it's written. A practical consequence is that calling df.filter(...) alone does nothing observable at all; nothing actually runs until something like df.filter(...).count() reaches an action.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it as the difference between writing a recipe and actually cooking. Every transformation I chain -- filter, select, withColumn -- just adds a line to the recipe; Spark doesn't touch any data yet, it's just building up a plan of what to do. The moment I call an action like count() or write(), Spark finally reads that whole recipe and executes it all at once, which lets it optimize the entire chain together rather than running each step the moment I write it. The thing that catches people off guard the first time is that if I write df.filter(col('Amount') > 100) on its own line and nothing happens, that's completely expected -- filter is a transformation, so Spark hasn't actually done anything yet. It's also why re-running count() on the same unchained DataFrame twice re-executes the whole plan from scratch, unless I've explicitly cached it.
commonMistakes: Expecting a transformation like filter() to immediately scan or change the data
Not realizing an error inside a transformation chain might not surface until an action is finally called
Calling an action repeatedly and being surprised the whole plan reruns each time instead of being remembered automatically
Confusing show() (an action that returns results) with a transformation, since it looks similar to printing a DataFrame
keyPoints: Transformations build a logical plan lazily; they don't touch data when called
Actions trigger Spark to actually execute the accumulated plan
Lazy evaluation lets Spark optimize the whole chain before running anything
Nothing observable happens until an action is reached; the plan re-executes each time an action is called unless cached

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes transformations from actions
Explains lazy evaluation and why Spark waits for an action
Gives correct examples of each

questions.title: Data governance vs. data management vs. data quality
questions.prompt: What's the practical difference between data governance, data management, and data quality? How do the three relate to each other rather than being three names for the same thing?
questions.modelAnswer: Data governance is the set of policies, decision rights, and accountability structures that determine who can do what with data -- the rules of the game. Data management is the actual day-to-day operational work of storing, moving, transforming, and maintaining data -- the doing. Data quality is a measurable outcome -- how fit-for-use the data actually is along dimensions like completeness and accuracy -- that governance aims to protect and that management's work directly affects. Governance sets the rules management operates under, and data quality is one of the concrete things governance uses to judge whether the whole system is actually working, rather than the three being interchangeable labels for the same activity.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd use a concrete chain to separate them: governance says 'revenue figures must be reviewed and approved by Finance before being published to executives' -- that's a policy, a rule about who's allowed to do what. Data management is the ETL team actually building and running the pipeline that loads and transforms the revenue data every night -- the operational work the policy applies to. Data quality is whether the number that pipeline produces is actually accurate and complete when someone looks at it on a dashboard. If I only focus on data management, I can build a technically working pipeline that still produces untrustworthy numbers because no one ever defined or enforced the rules around it -- which is exactly the gap governance exists to close.
commonMistakes: Using 'governance,' 'management,' and 'quality' interchangeably as if they were synonyms
Treating data quality work as separate from governance instead of as a measurable outcome governance cares about
Assuming governance is purely an IT or compliance function rather than something that shapes day-to-day operational work
Thinking data management happens in a vacuum, with no policy or accountability guiding it
keyPoints: Governance = policy and decision rights (the rules)
Management = operational execution (the doing)
Quality = a measurable outcome governance aims to protect
The three work together as a system, not as synonyms for the same activity

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines all three terms distinctly
Explains how the three relate to and depend on each other
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: Data owner vs. data steward
questions.prompt: What's the difference between a data owner and a data steward in a data governance program? Who's typically accountable for a dataset, and who does the hands-on work of maintaining its quality and definitions?
questions.modelAnswer: A data owner is typically a senior business role -- a VP of Sales owning the 'Customer' domain, for example -- who holds ultimate accountability for a data domain: approving policy, approving access, and being answerable for outcomes, even though they usually aren't doing hands-on work themselves. A data steward is the person who actually does that hands-on, operational work: maintaining definitions, monitoring quality, resolving day-to-day issues, and enforcing the owner's policies in practice. The relationship is accountable versus responsible -- the owner is accountable for the domain overall and makes the bigger calls, while the steward is responsible for the daily maintenance and escalates anything bigger back up to the owner.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe a real pairing: the VP of Sales owns the 'Customer' domain -- if something goes badly wrong with customer data, that's ultimately their accountability. A senior sales-ops analyst acts as the steward -- they're the one actually keeping the Customer glossary definitions current, watching the quality dashboard, and fixing or escalating issues as they come up day to day. The steward doesn't need to go to the owner for every small fix, but if there's a genuinely contested decision -- like two departments disagreeing on what 'Active Customer' means -- that's exactly the kind of call that needs to go up to the owner, because the steward doesn't have the authority to settle it alone.
commonMistakes: Conflating owner and steward as if they were the same role with two names
Assuming the owner is expected to do hands-on data maintenance work themselves
Appointing a steward with no backing from an accountable owner, leaving them with responsibility but no authority to actually enforce fixes
Assuming only IT holds these roles, when the owner in particular is usually a business role
keyPoints: Owner = accountable, usually a senior business role
Steward = responsible for hands-on, day-to-day maintenance
Stewards need the owner's backing to actually enforce decisions
Both roles exist together -- neither one substitutes for the other

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes owner (accountable) from steward (responsible/operational)
Gives a credible real-world example of the pairing
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: Completeness, accuracy, and validity at a glance
questions.prompt: What's the difference between completeness, accuracy, and validity as data quality dimensions? Give an example of a record that could be complete and valid but still inaccurate.
questions.modelAnswer: Completeness is whether a required value is present at all -- no missing or null fields. Validity is whether a value conforms to an expected format or rule -- a phone number has the right number of digits, a state code is a real postal abbreviation. Accuracy is whether the value is actually true in reality, independent of whether it's present or well-formatted. A customer record can be complete (every field is filled in) and valid (the phone number is a well-formed 10-digit number) and still be inaccurate -- if it's the customer's old phone number that's no longer correct, it passes both checks while still being wrong.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through the same record against all three dimensions to show they're independent. Completeness just asks 'is anything blank' -- a phone field with something in it passes. Validity asks 'does what's there look like a real phone number' -- ten digits, correct format, it passes that too. Neither of those checks can tell me whether that specific number still actually reaches the customer -- that's accuracy, and it usually requires comparing against some external, trusted signal, not just examining the value in isolation. I treat passing completeness and validity checks as necessary groundwork, not proof the data is correct -- a record can sail through both and still be dead wrong.
questions.example:
Record: Phone = '555-201-8834' (10-digit, well-formed, non-blank)
Completeness: PASS -- a value is present
Validity: PASS -- matches the expected phone format
Accuracy: FAIL -- it's the customer's disconnected old number, no longer correct
commonMistakes: Assuming a value that passes a validity/format check must also be accurate
Treating completeness as the only quality dimension worth checking
Not realizing accuracy often requires comparing against an external source of truth, which internal profiling alone can't confirm
Using 'complete,' 'valid,' and 'accurate' interchangeably as if they mean the same thing
keyPoints: Completeness = presence (is a value there at all)
Validity = conformance to an expected format or rule
Accuracy = actually true in the real world, independent of format or presence
A record can pass completeness and validity checks and still be inaccurate

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines all three dimensions distinctly
Gives a correct example showing complete + valid but inaccurate
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: Business glossary vs. data dictionary
questions.prompt: What's the difference between a business glossary and a data dictionary? If a report shows a metric called 'Active Customer,' which of the two would define what that term means in plain business language, and which would describe the actual database column(s) behind it?
questions.modelAnswer: A business glossary holds business-facing, plain-language definitions of business terms and concepts -- what 'Active Customer' means to the business, such as a customer with a purchase in the last 12 months -- independent of any specific system or table, and typically owned and approved by the business. A data dictionary documents the actual technical structure: table names, column names, data types, and constraints, describing the physical implementation, which may map to one or more glossary terms. The glossary answers 'what does this term mean to the business'; the dictionary answers 'what table and column actually stores it.'
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd use 'Active Customer' directly. The glossary entry says, in plain language, what counts as active, why, and who owns that definition -- no mention of any specific table. The data dictionary entry is completely different: it documents the actual IsActiveFlag column in the Customer table -- its data type, whether it's nullable, what values it allows -- which is the physical thing that implements the glossary's business rule. The glossary and the dictionary need to be linked to each other, because a business definition with nothing backing it in the actual data is just a nice sentence, and a documented column with no business definition behind it is just a schema note nobody can interpret.
commonMistakes: Treating the glossary and the dictionary as the same document with two names
Starting with the technical documentation before the business ever agrees on a definition
Writing glossary entries that describe technical fields instead of business concepts
Leaving a glossary term with no link to any actual underlying data that implements it
keyPoints: Glossary = business meaning in plain language
Dictionary = technical structure (tables, columns, types)
The same real-world concept needs both, linked together
A glossary term should be defined independent of any single system

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes the glossary from the dictionary
Applies the distinction correctly to the Active Customer example
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: What makes a data element 'critical'
questions.prompt: What is a critical data element (CDE), and why would a governance program choose to focus its limited attention on a small set of CDEs rather than trying to govern every single column in every system equally?
questions.modelAnswer: A critical data element is a data element whose accuracy and quality carry material business, financial, or regulatory impact if it's wrong -- things like an account balance, revenue figure, or a regulatory reporting field -- as opposed to the vast majority of fields where a small error causes little real harm. Because stewards' time, monitoring tooling, and review processes are all finite resources, effective governance programs deliberately prioritize: identify which fields carry the highest risk or impact, and concentrate rigorous definition, quality monitoring, and stewardship there first, rather than trying to govern thousands of columns uniformly, which in practice usually means governing none of them well.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame it as a budget problem. A typical table might have fifty columns, but realistically only three to five of them are things a regulator, an auditor, or an executive would actually care about if they went wrong. If I spread governance attention evenly across all fifty, I end up with shallow, token effort on everything and genuine rigor on nothing. If I instead identify the handful that are genuinely critical -- usually tied to financial reporting, regulatory obligations, or core business decisions -- I can give those the real stewardship, monitoring, and documentation they need, and let the rest get a lighter-touch standard. I also revisit that CDE list periodically, because what counts as critical shifts as the business and regulatory landscape changes.
commonMistakes: Trying to treat every column as equally critical, spreading effort too thin to be effective anywhere
Never revisiting the CDE list as business priorities or regulatory requirements change
Picking CDEs based on technical complexity rather than actual business, financial, or regulatory impact
Designating something critical without documenting why, making the list hard to defend or maintain later
keyPoints: A CDE carries material business, financial, or regulatory impact if it's wrong
Governance resources are finite, so prioritization is necessary
CDEs get the most rigorous definition, monitoring, and stewardship
The CDE list should be reviewed periodically, not treated as fixed forever

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines a critical data element
Explains the rationale for prioritizing a small set over uniform coverage
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: What data lineage actually tracks
questions.prompt: What is data lineage, in plain terms? If a number on an executive dashboard looks wrong, what question is lineage specifically meant to help you answer that a data quality check alone can't?
questions.modelAnswer: Data lineage is the traceable record of where a piece of data came from, every system and transformation step it passed through, and where it ends up -- essentially a map of a data element's journey from source to final report. A data quality check can tell you a number looks wrong -- it fails a rule, is missing, or is out of range -- but it doesn't by itself tell you why or where in the pipeline it went wrong. Lineage answers that follow-up question: given this suspicious number on the dashboard, which upstream source, transformation step, or load actually produced it, so you know exactly where to go look.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd separate the two jobs clearly. A quality check is what flags that revenue dropped 40 percent overnight and that's worth investigating. Lineage is what actually lets me walk backward from that dashboard tile to the semantic model behind it, to the warehouse table feeding the model, to the ETL job that loaded it, to the source system the job pulled from -- finding exactly which link in that chain actually broke. Without documented lineage, that same investigation turns into manually asking around and guessing, which is slow and unreliable compared to just looking up a maintained map of the pipeline.
commonMistakes: Confusing lineage with data quality checking, when the two answer different questions
Treating lineage as only a nice-to-have diagram rather than an active troubleshooting and impact-analysis tool
Assuming lineage only matters for compliance or audit purposes, not day-to-day troubleshooting
Not maintaining lineage documentation, so tracing a bad number back to its source takes hours of manual digging
keyPoints: Lineage is the traceable path a piece of data takes from source to final report
A quality check flags that something's wrong; lineage helps find where
Lineage supports both troubleshooting and impact analysis
Without lineage, tracing a bad number back to its source is slow and manual

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines data lineage
Correctly distinguishes lineage's role from a data quality check's role
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, and DENSE_RANK side by side
questions.prompt: Write a query that ranks products by ListPrice descending using ROW_NUMBER(), RANK(), and DENSE_RANK() in the same result set, and explain how the three functions differ when two products are tied for the same price.
questions.modelAnswer: ROW_NUMBER() always produces unique, sequential numbers — even for genuinely tied values, it arbitrarily breaks the tie and gives one row a lower number than the other. RANK() gives tied rows the same number, but leaves a gap afterward: if two products tie for rank 1, the next distinct price gets rank 3, not 2, because RANK() accounts for how many rows were tied at the previous rank. DENSE_RANK() also gives tied rows the same number, but with no gap — the next distinct price after a tie at rank 1 gets rank 2. All three are computed with an OVER (ORDER BY ...) window clause and require no GROUP BY.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd run all three in one query so the difference is visible directly in the output rather than just described. If two products are tied for the most expensive, ROW_NUMBER() pretends there's no tie at all and numbers them 1 and 2 arbitrarily — which would misrepresent a genuine tie as a win. RANK() is honest about the tie: both get rank 1, but the next product jumps to rank 3, because two rows already occupied rank 1's 'slot.' DENSE_RANK() is also honest about the tie — both get rank 1 — but it only cares about distinct values, so the next price tier is rank 2 with no gap. Which one I pick depends on the business question: a sales leaderboard where two reps tied for second place genuinely skips third place calls for RANK(); a scale of distinct price tiers where I just want the next gap-free tier number calls for DENSE_RANK().
questions.example:
SELECT Name, ListPrice,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY ListPrice DESC) AS RowNum,
       RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY ListPrice DESC) AS Rank_,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY ListPrice DESC) AS DenseRank_
FROM Production.Product
ORDER BY ListPrice DESC;
-- Tied prices: RowNum stays unique, Rank_ ties then skips ahead,
-- DenseRank_ ties with no gap.
commonMistakes: Assuming ROW_NUMBER() is 'safer' for ties when it actually hides them by assigning arbitrary unique numbers
Confusing RANK's gap-after-a-tie behavior with DENSE_RANK's no-gap behavior
Forgetting that ORDER BY inside OVER() determines which rows get which rank — changing it changes the whole result
Trying to use these functions without an OVER() clause, or expecting them to need a GROUP BY
keyPoints: ROW_NUMBER() always produces unique numbers, even for ties
RANK() ties share a number but the next value skips ahead by the tie size
DENSE_RANK() ties share a number with no gap for the next distinct value
All three run inside OVER (ORDER BY ...), no GROUP BY needed

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct syntax for all three ranking functions
Accurately explains the tie-handling difference
Picks a sensible real-world scenario for each function

questions.title: Write a parameterized stored procedure
questions.prompt: Write a stored procedure named usp_GetProductsAbovePrice that accepts a @MinPrice parameter defaulting to 100, and returns the Name and ListPrice of every product in Production.Product with a ListPrice at or above that value, ordered by price descending. Then show how you'd call it both with and without supplying a value for @MinPrice.
questions.modelAnswer: A parameter is declared right after the procedure name, before the AS keyword, and behaves like a normal variable throughout the procedure body — it's just pre-populated from whatever the caller passes in. Giving a parameter a default value (@MinPrice MONEY = 100) makes it optional: if the caller doesn't supply a value, SQL Server uses the default automatically. Calling the procedure with named notation (EXEC usp_GetProductsAbovePrice @MinPrice = 500) is unambiguous and order-independent, which is why it's preferred over positional calling once a procedure has more than one parameter.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write the parameter with a sensible default so the procedure is usable both ways out of the box. The body itself is just the same filtered, sorted SELECT I'd write ad hoc, except @MinPrice stands in for whatever literal value I'd otherwise hard-code. Calling it with EXEC usp_GetProductsAbovePrice; uses the default of 100 automatically, and calling it with @MinPrice = 500 overrides that for just this call. I always call with named parameters -- @MinPrice = 500 instead of just 500 -- because the moment a procedure picks up a second or third parameter, positional calling becomes an easy way to silently pass values to the wrong parameter.
questions.example:
CREATE PROCEDURE usp_GetProductsAbovePrice
    @MinPrice MONEY = 100
AS
BEGIN
    SELECT Name, ListPrice
    FROM Production.Product
    WHERE ListPrice >= @MinPrice
    ORDER BY ListPrice DESC;
END;
GO

EXEC usp_GetProductsAbovePrice @MinPrice = 500; -- overrides the default
EXEC usp_GetProductsAbovePrice;                 -- uses the default, 100
commonMistakes: Forgetting the default value, which forces every caller to always supply @MinPrice even when a sensible default exists
Calling the procedure positionally once it has multiple parameters, risking values landing in the wrong parameter
Putting the parameter declaration after AS instead of before it
Hard-coding the price threshold inside the procedure body instead of parameterizing it, defeating the point of a reusable procedure
keyPoints: Parameters are declared before AS and behave like pre-populated variables
A default value makes a parameter optional
Named notation (@Param = value) is unambiguous and order-independent
EXEC without a value for an optional parameter falls back to its default

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct CREATE PROCEDURE syntax with a default parameter
Correct query logic (filter + sort)
Shows both calling styles (with and without override)

questions.title: Write a basic nonclustered index
questions.prompt: Write a T-SQL statement that creates a nonclustered index on the OrderDate column of a Sales.Orders table, and explain at a high level why an index on a frequently-filtered column speeds up a query.
questions.code: -- Goal: CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX ... ON Sales.Orders (OrderDate)
questions.modelAnswer: CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Orders_OrderDate ON Sales.Orders (OrderDate); builds a separate, smaller structure that's sorted by OrderDate and holds a pointer back to each full row. A query that filters on OrderDate can then seek directly to the matching range inside that small sorted structure instead of scanning every row in the table just to check each one's OrderDate — that's the practical difference between an index seek and a full table scan, and it's the reason the same query can go from checking every row to checking only the handful that actually match.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Orders_OrderDate ON Sales.Orders (OrderDate); and explain it as giving SQL Server a shortcut: instead of reading the whole table row by row to find which ones fall in a given date range, it can jump straight into this much smaller, OrderDate-sorted structure, find the matching range, and use the pointers stored there to go get just those specific rows. That's an index seek instead of a table scan, and on a large table that difference can be the entire performance story for a query. I'd also be upfront that this isn't free — every index adds overhead to every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE that touches OrderDate, so it's a tradeoff, not a universal win.
questions.example:
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Orders_OrderDate
ON Sales.Orders (OrderDate);
commonMistakes: Assuming every column should be indexed, ignoring the write-cost an index adds
Forgetting a nonclustered index is a separate structure, not a physical reordering of the table itself (only the clustered index does that)
Expecting an index to help a query that doesn't actually filter or sort on an indexed column
Not giving the index a meaningful, identifiable name
keyPoints: CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX syntax targets a specific column
An index is a separate, smaller sorted structure plus a pointer back to the full row
It enables an index seek instead of a full table scan on a filtered query
Indexes have a write-cost on every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE that touches the indexed column

Correctly explains seek vs. scan

questions.title: Read a CSV into a DataFrame and filter it
questions.prompt: Write PySpark code that reads a CSV file located at '/mnt/raw/orders.csv' (with a header row) into a DataFrame, then returns only the rows where the Amount column is greater than 100.
questions.code:
# spark is an existing SparkSession
# File: /mnt/raw/orders.csv, has a header row, includes a numeric Amount column
questions.modelAnswer: Reading a CSV correctly requires two options: header, so the first row is treated as column names instead of data, and inferSchema, so numeric columns like Amount are read as actual numbers rather than strings (without it, every column defaults to string, and a numeric comparison like > 100 either fails or compares lexically instead of numerically). filter() is a transformation — it builds a step in the logical plan but doesn't execute anything on its own; an action like show() or count() is what actually triggers Spark to read the file and apply the filter.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd read it as spark.read.option('header', 'true').option('inferSchema', 'true').csv('/mnt/raw/orders.csv'), then filter with df.filter(col('Amount') > 100). The two options matter more than they look: without header, Spark treats the column names themselves as a data row; without inferSchema, Amount comes in as a string, and depending on the Spark version that numeric-looking comparison either throws an error or silently does a string comparison that doesn't mean what I want. I'd remember that filter() alone doesn't do anything observable — I'd need to call something like .show() or .count() afterward to actually see the filtered rows, since Spark doesn't read or process the file until an action forces it to.
questions.example:
from pyspark.sql.functions import col

df = (
    spark.read
    .option("header", "true")
    .option("inferSchema", "true")
    .csv("/mnt/raw/orders.csv")
)

high_value_orders = df.filter(col("Amount") > 100)
high_value_orders.show()
commonMistakes: Forgetting the header option, which causes the header row itself to be read as a data row
Forgetting inferSchema, leaving every column as a string and breaking a numeric comparison
Calling filter() and expecting to see results immediately, without an action like show() or count()
Comparing Amount to the string "100" instead of the integer 100 once the column is correctly typed as numeric
keyPoints: spark.read needs header and inferSchema options set correctly for a CSV with a numeric column
filter() takes a Column expression, usually built with col()
filter() is lazy — nothing executes until an action like show() or count() is called
Without inferSchema, numeric comparisons on a CSV-sourced column can behave incorrectly

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct read syntax with header/schema options
Correct filter syntax and logic
Explains the lazy evaluation implication

questions.title: Write a SQL completeness-profiling query
questions.prompt: Write a T-SQL query against a Customers table that calculates the completeness percentage of the Email column — the percentage of rows where Email is not NULL and not an empty string.
questions.modelAnswer: The query needs a total row count and a count of rows where Email actually has a usable value, then divides one by the other. A completeness check has to catch both ways a value can be 'missing' -- genuinely NULL, and a non-NULL but empty string, which many source systems produce instead of a true NULL. Dividing two integer counts in T-SQL truncates to an integer unless at least one side is cast to a decimal or float type first, so the percentage calculation needs an explicit CAST to avoid silently getting 0 or 100 instead of a real percentage like 87.42.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write COUNT(*) for the denominator and SUM(CASE WHEN Email IS NOT NULL AND Email <> '' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) for the numerator, then compute the percentage with an explicit CAST to DECIMAL so the division doesn't truncate. I always check for both NULL and empty string specifically because I've been burned before by a source system that writes '' instead of a true NULL for a missing field -- a completeness check that only looks for IS NULL would silently miss every one of those and report a falsely high score. I'd also round the result to something readable, like two decimal places, before putting it on any kind of report.
questions.example:
SELECT
    COUNT(*) AS TotalRows,
    SUM(CASE WHEN Email IS NOT NULL AND Email <> '' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS NonBlankRows,
    CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN Email IS NOT NULL AND Email <> '' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS DECIMAL(5,2))
        / COUNT(*) * 100 AS CompletenessPct
FROM dbo.Customers;
commonMistakes: Checking only for NULL and missing blank/empty-string values that should also count as incomplete
Letting integer division truncate the percentage to 0 or 100 instead of casting to a decimal type
Not rounding or formatting the result for a readable report
Running the check once instead of scheduling it to run on a recurring basis to catch regressions
keyPoints: Completeness % = non-blank rows divided by total rows
A completeness check must catch both NULL and empty-string values
Cast to a decimal type before dividing to avoid integer-division truncation
Profiling queries like this are the simplest kind of automatable quality check

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct query logic computing a completeness percentage
Correctly handles both NULL and empty-string blanks
Avoids integer-division truncation

questions.title: Write a SQL duplicate-detection query
questions.prompt: Write a T-SQL query that finds every Email value in a Customers table that appears on more than one row, along with how many times each duplicated value occurs.
questions.modelAnswer: The standard pattern is GROUP BY Email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 -- grouping collapses rows sharing the same Email into one group per value, and HAVING then filters down to only the groups with more than one row in them, which is exactly what a duplicate is. This checks the uniqueness dimension: whether a value that's supposed to identify something distinctly is actually distinct. NULL Email values need separate thought, since multiple NULLs grouping together don't necessarily represent a meaningful 'duplicate' the way two identical real email addresses do.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write SELECT Email, COUNT(*) AS Occurrences FROM dbo.Customers WHERE Email IS NOT NULL GROUP BY Email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 ORDER BY Occurrences DESC. Excluding NULL up front keeps the result focused on genuine duplicate values rather than mixing in however many customers simply have no email on file. This is usually the first thing I run after merging customer data from two source systems, since that's exactly the scenario that tends to introduce real duplicates -- the same person existing as two separate rows because each system had its own copy before the merge.
questions.example:
SELECT Email, COUNT(*) AS Occurrences
FROM dbo.Customers
WHERE Email IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY Email
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY Occurrences DESC;
commonMistakes: Forgetting HAVING is required here -- WHERE can't filter on an aggregate like COUNT()
Not excluding or separately handling NULL Email values, which can misleadingly look like duplicates
Stopping at detection without pulling the full duplicate rows for actual review
Assuming uniqueness problems only occur on primary keys, when business keys like email or SSN are often the ones that actually matter
keyPoints: GROUP BY plus HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 is the standard duplicate-finding pattern
Uniqueness violations often surface after merging data from multiple source systems
NULLs need separate handling rather than being treated as meaningful duplicates
Detecting duplicates is step one -- investigating and remediating is separate follow-up work

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct GROUP BY / HAVING syntax for finding duplicates
Correctly handles NULL values
Explains a realistic scenario where this check matters

questions.title: Write a SQL orphan-record check
questions.prompt: Write a T-SQL query that finds every row in an Orders table whose CustomerID does not exist in the Customers table — i.e., an orphaned order with no matching customer.
questions.modelAnswer: This uses the LEFT JOIN plus IS NULL pattern: LEFT JOIN Orders to Customers on CustomerID, then filter WHERE Customers.CustomerID IS NULL, which only happens when no matching customer row exists. This is a referential integrity quality check used specifically where there's no enforced foreign key constraint doing this automatically -- common in a data warehouse, where FK constraints are often deliberately skipped for load-performance reasons, or when loading from source systems that never enforced one.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write a LEFT JOIN from Orders to Customers on CustomerID, then filter to where the Customers side came back NULL -- that's the signature of an order with no matching customer. I reach for this constantly on warehouse tables specifically because many data warehouses intentionally don't enforce foreign keys the way an OLTP system would, for load-speed reasons, which means nothing is stopping an orphaned row from existing unless I go looking for it myself with a query like this. I'd avoid using NOT IN for this instead of the LEFT JOIN, since NOT IN has a well-known trap where a single NULL in the subquery's result silently makes the whole NOT IN return no rows at all.
questions.example:
SELECT o.OrderID, o.CustomerID
FROM dbo.Orders AS o
LEFT JOIN dbo.Customers AS c
    ON o.CustomerID = c.CustomerID
WHERE c.CustomerID IS NULL;
commonMistakes: Assuming a formal FK constraint makes this check unnecessary, when many warehouse tables deliberately don't enforce one
Using NOT IN instead of LEFT JOIN plus IS NULL, running into NOT IN's well-known NULL-handling trap
Not also checking the reverse direction when it's relevant to the question being asked
Running this once instead of scheduling it as a recurring quality check
keyPoints: LEFT JOIN plus IS NULL is the standard orphan-record detection pattern
Referential integrity checks matter most where no FK constraint is actually enforced
NOT IN has a NULL-handling pitfall that the LEFT JOIN approach avoids
This should run as a recurring check, not a one-time investigation

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct LEFT JOIN / IS NULL syntax for finding orphan rows
Explains why this matters most where no FK constraint exists
Avoids or flags the NOT IN / NULL pitfall

questions.title: Draft a business glossary entry
questions.prompt: Write a business glossary entry for the term 'Active Customer,' including a plain-language definition, the business rule that determines who qualifies, and the role that should own/approve it. Explain why a vague definition like 'a customer who is active' isn't good enough.
questions.modelAnswer: A usable glossary entry needs three things: a plain-language definition, a concrete business rule that's actually testable, and a named owner responsible for approving it. For 'Active Customer': Definition -- a customer who has made at least one purchase within the trailing 12 months. Business Rule -- LastPurchaseDate is on or after 12 months before today, and the customer's status is not Closed. Owner -- the VP of Sales, as accountable owner of the Customer domain. 'A customer who is active' is circular and unusable because it doesn't specify a time window, doesn't specify a data source, and leaves every team to interpret it differently -- which is exactly how two departments end up publishing two different numbers for the same term.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't publish a term until it has all three pieces. I'd draft the plain-language definition first, then turn it into an actual testable rule -- LastPurchaseDate within the last 12 months, status not Closed -- specific enough that two different people implementing it in SQL would produce the same result. I'd route it to the Customer domain's owner for approval before treating it as authoritative, and I'd explicitly think through edge cases up front, like what happens to a customer who returned their only purchase, rather than leaving that ambiguous and letting each report builder guess differently.
questions.example:
Term: Active Customer
Definition: A customer who has made at least one purchase in the trailing 12 months.
Business Rule: LastPurchaseDate >= DATEADD(month, -12, GETDATE()) AND Status <> 'Closed'
Owner: VP of Sales (Customer domain)
Status: Approved
commonMistakes: Writing a circular, vague definition with no measurable rule behind it
Skipping the step of naming an owner, leaving no one able to approve changes or resolve disputes
Leaving out the specific business rule or threshold, forcing every report builder to guess
Not accounting for edge cases, like a reactivated customer or a returned purchase
keyPoints: A good glossary entry pairs a plain-language definition with a concrete, testable business rule
Every term needs a named owner for approval and disputes
Vague definitions are a leading cause of conflicting reports showing different numbers
Edge cases should be explicitly addressed, not left implicit

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Writes a clear, plain-language definition
Writes a specific, testable business rule
Names an owner and explains why vague definitions fail

questions.title: Document a table column in a data dictionary
questions.prompt: Write a data dictionary entry for the OrderStatus column of an Orders table: the kind of technical and descriptive information a good data dictionary entry should capture, filled in with a plausible real example.
questions.modelAnswer: A good data dictionary entry captures both technical facts and descriptive business context, not just the raw type. For OrderStatus: Table -- Orders; Data Type -- VARCHAR(20); Nullable -- No; Allowed Values -- 'Pending', 'Shipped', 'Delivered', 'Cancelled'; Description -- the current fulfillment status of the order; Source System -- the OrderEntry application; Load Frequency -- nightly ETL. Capturing allowed values and business meaning alongside the raw type is what distinguishes a real data dictionary entry from simply exporting the database schema.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd document both halves deliberately. The technical half -- VARCHAR(20), not nullable -- is easy, it comes straight from the schema. The half that actually takes effort is the descriptive side: what the column means, where it's sourced from, and specifically the allowed values, because that list is what lets me catch an unexpected new status code showing up later instead of just shrugging at it. I'd also record the source system, since that's exactly the detail someone doing a root-cause investigation later will need in order to trace a bad value back to where it actually originated.
questions.example:
Table: Orders
Column: OrderStatus
Data Type: VARCHAR(20)
Nullable: No
Allowed Values: Pending, Shipped, Delivered, Cancelled
Description: Current fulfillment status of the order
Source System: OrderEntry application
Load Frequency: Nightly ETL
Last Reviewed: 2026-10-01
commonMistakes: Documenting only the data type and skipping allowed values or business meaning, essentially re-exporting the schema
Leaving the entry unowned, so nobody updates it when the column's valid values change
Not noting the source system, making a later root-cause investigation harder
Letting dictionary entries go stale as the schema evolves, with no last-reviewed date
keyPoints: A data dictionary entry needs both technical facts and business context
Allowed-values documentation helps catch invalid or unexpected data later
Recording the source system supports later lineage and troubleshooting work
Entries need a review cadence so they don't go stale

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Captures the technical facts (type, nullability, constraints)
Captures business context (meaning, allowed values, source system)
Explains why both halves matter, not just the schema export

questions.title: Map a simple source-to-report lineage path
questions.prompt: A 'Total Revenue' tile on an executive Power BI dashboard pulls from a semantic model, which is built from a warehouse table, which is loaded nightly by an ETL job from an OrderEntry source system. Write out that lineage as a simple source-to-report chain, and explain what you'd want documented at each link.
questions.modelAnswer: The chain runs: OrderEntry source system (the raw table/column holding order amounts) -> nightly ETL job (what transformation or aggregation happens) -> warehouse table (the grain stored, such as daily revenue by region) -> semantic model (the measure definition, including any filters applied) -> the Power BI 'Total Revenue' tile. At each link, the documentation should capture what the step actually does, when it runs, and any business rule or filter applied, so an investigator can walk the chain in either direction later without having to ask around.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd treat this like drawing a simple left-to-right diagram with boxes and arrows: OrderEntry.Orders.Amount feeds the nightly ETL job, which lands in Warehouse.FactRevenue, which the semantic model turns into a TotalRevenue measure, which the dashboard tile displays. I'd be just as careful documenting the semantic-model layer as the raw source -- that measure's exact definition, including any filters, is often where two reports quietly disagree, and it's the link people are most likely to skip documenting because it feels like 'just a formula' rather than a real step in the chain.
questions.example:
OrderEntry.Orders.Amount
  -> ETL_NightlyLoad (aggregates daily, converts currency)
  -> Warehouse.FactRevenue (grain: daily revenue by region)
  -> SemanticModel.TotalRevenue (measure: SUM of Amount, filtered to closed orders)
  -> Dashboard.TotalRevenueTile
commonMistakes: Only documenting the two endpoints (source and report) and skipping the intermediate transformation steps
Not recording what a transformation step actually does, just that it exists
Treating lineage as a one-time diagram instead of something to keep current as the pipeline changes
Skipping the business rule or filter at the semantic-model layer, where many report discrepancies actually originate
keyPoints: Lineage is a chain of links from source to final report, not just two endpoints
Each link should document what it does, when it runs, and any business rule applied
The semantic-model/measure layer is a common, often under-documented source of discrepancies
Lineage documentation needs to be kept current as pipelines evolve

Identifies what should be documented at each link
Flags the semantic-model/measure layer as a key documentation point

questions.title: Debugging a WHERE = NULL mistake
questions.prompt: A junior developer writes WHERE MiddleName = NULL to find customers with no middle name recorded, and gets zero rows back — even though many customers genuinely have a NULL MiddleName. What's actually wrong with that query, and how should they fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: NULL represents an unknown or not-applicable value, not zero or an empty string. Because it's unknown, NULL can't be said to equal anything — not even another NULL — so any comparison using the = operator against NULL evaluates to unknown (treated as false), never true. That means WHERE MiddleName = NULL will always return zero rows, regardless of how many rows actually have a NULL MiddleName, because the comparison can never succeed. The fix is to use the special IS NULL syntax instead: WHERE MiddleName IS NULL. IS NULL isn't a comparison operator — it's dedicated syntax built specifically to test for the absence of a value, and it works correctly where = cannot. The same logic applies to IS NOT NULL for the opposite case.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd point out is that this isn't a typo or syntax error — the query runs fine, it just silently returns the wrong answer, which is the dangerous kind of bug. I'd explain that NULL means 'unknown,' and you can't compare an unknown value to anything using = and expect a meaningful true or false — SQL Server treats that comparison as unknown, which gets filtered out just like false. So WHERE MiddleName = NULL isn't matching NULLs, it's failing to match anything at all. The fix is WHERE MiddleName IS NULL, which is purpose-built syntax for exactly this case rather than a regular comparison. If the goal were actually to display something readable instead of filtering, I'd reach for ISNULL(MiddleName, '(none)') or COALESCE for more than two fallback values.
commonMistakes: Not realizing the query runs without error and silently returns the wrong result, rather than throwing an obvious failure
Treating NULL as if it were an empty string or zero instead of 'unknown'
Using = NULL or <> NULL anywhere instead of IS NULL / IS NOT NULL
Confusing ISNULL() (replaces a NULL with a default, two arguments) with IS NULL (tests for NULL)
keyPoints: NULL means unknown/not applicable, not zero or empty string
= NULL always evaluates to unknown/false, never true
IS NULL / IS NOT NULL is the only correct way to test for NULL
ISNULL()/COALESCE() substitute a default value rather than test for NULL

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses why = NULL fails silently
Provides the correct fix (IS NULL)
Mentions ISNULL/COALESCE as a related but different tool

questions.title: Diagnosing an accidental Cartesian product
questions.prompt: A query joining a 500-row Products table to a 100,000-row OrderDetail table unexpectedly returns 50 million rows instead of something in the few-hundred-thousand range. What almost certainly went wrong, and how would you confirm it?
questions.modelAnswer: 50 million is exactly 500 times 100,000 -- the row-count signature of a Cartesian product, where every row of one table gets paired with every row of the other instead of only matching rows being paired. The most common real-world cause isn't a deliberate CROSS JOIN -- it's a missing or ineffective ON condition on what was meant to be a normal join: either the ON clause is left out entirely (old-style comma join with no join condition), or it exists but evaluates to true for nearly every row combination (for example ON p.Name IS NOT NULL, which doesn't actually relate the two tables). To confirm it, check the join's ON clause first for a missing or non-relating condition, and as a general habit, sanity-check the row count after any join: if two tables of roughly 500 and 100,000 rows produce millions of result rows instead of a number in that rough range, that's an immediate signal to re-check the ON clause rather than assume the data is simply that large.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd notice is that 50 million is suspiciously close to 500 times 100,000 -- that's the fingerprint of a Cartesian product, not a coincidence. My first move is to go straight to the ON clause of the join and check two things: is it missing entirely, which happens with old comma-style joins that have no join condition at all, or does it exist but not actually relate the two tables -- something like ON p.Name IS NOT NULL, which is true for almost every row and produces a Cartesian product in disguise even though there's technically an ON clause sitting there. Once I fix the condition to something that actually ties the tables together, like p.ProductID = sod.ProductID, I'd re-run the query and expect the row count to land in the same rough range as the bigger of the two tables, not multiply them together. I've made this a habit on every join I write now: sanity-check the row count before trusting the result.
questions.example:
-- BUG: no join condition at all -- a Cartesian product
SELECT p.Name, sod.OrderQty
FROM Production.Product AS p, Sales.SalesOrderDetail AS sod;

-- BUG: ON clause exists but doesn't relate the tables
SELECT p.Name, sod.OrderQty
FROM Production.Product AS p
INNER JOIN Sales.SalesOrderDetail AS sod
    ON p.Name IS NOT NULL;

-- FIXED: a real join condition tying the tables together
SELECT p.Name, sod.OrderQty
FROM Production.Product AS p
INNER JOIN Sales.SalesOrderDetail AS sod
    ON p.ProductID = sod.ProductID;
commonMistakes: Assuming the data itself is just 'that big' instead of suspecting the join condition first
Not recognizing that an ON clause can exist and still produce a Cartesian product if it doesn't genuinely relate the tables
Never sanity-checking row counts after writing a join, so the problem isn't caught until it hits production
Confusing this with a deliberate CROSS JOIN -- the accidental version almost always comes from a broken or missing ON condition on what was meant to be a normal join
keyPoints: Row count multiplying (500 x 100,000) instead of adding is the signature of a Cartesian product
Most accidental Cartesian products come from a missing or non-relating ON clause
Old-style comma joins with no ON clause default to a Cartesian product
An ON clause that's technically present but true for nearly every row is just as dangerous as none at all
Sanity-check row counts after any join as a standing habit

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the Cartesian product and the row-count math
Correctly identifies missing/ineffective ON clause as the cause
Describes a practical way to catch this before production

questions.title: SUM inflated after joining a one-to-many table
questions.prompt: A query joins SalesOrderHeader to SalesOrderDetail and correctly totals each order with SUM(LineTotal). After adding a third join to a Promotion table -- where some orders have more than one matching promotion row -- the total for those specific orders suddenly doubles or triples, even though nothing about the actual sales changed. The join conditions are all correct and genuinely relate the tables. What's going on, and how would you fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: This isn't a Cartesian product -- every join condition is correct and genuinely relates the tables -- it's join fan-out, which happens whenever a correct join still has a one-to-many relationship on one side. Each SalesOrderDetail row that matches more than one Promotion row gets physically duplicated once per matching promotion before SUM ever runs, so SUM(LineTotal) is now adding the same line total two or three times for any order whose promotion happens to match more than once, while orders with exactly one (or zero) matching promotions are unaffected. The fix is to never combine two separate one-to-many expansions in a single flat join and then aggregate at the end -- instead, pre-aggregate each one-to-many relationship to the grain actually needed, in its own subquery or CTE, before joining. Here, that means computing the order total from SalesOrderHeader and SalesOrderDetail alone first, and only joining Promotion afterward (or in a separate query) if promotion details are genuinely needed, rather than letting its fan-out multiply rows that feed directly into the order-total SUM.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd point out first that this isn't the Cartesian-product bug people usually learn about -- every join condition here is correct and really does relate the tables. This is fan-out: joining in a table that can legitimately match more than one row per order duplicates the order-detail rows underneath it, once per matching promotion, before the SUM even runs. So an order with two matching promotions gets its LineTotal counted twice, not because the math is wrong, but because the row genuinely got duplicated first. My fix is to separate the two aggregations: compute each order's total from just SalesOrderHeader and SalesOrderDetail in a CTE first, completely isolated from the Promotion join, and only bring Promotion into a separate query (or join it after the order total is already locked in) if I actually need promotion-level detail. The rule I'd apply going forward is never to let two independent one-to-many joins sit in the same flat query feeding one aggregate -- pre-aggregate each one to the grain I need first.
questions.example:
-- WRONG: Promotion's fan-out inflates the order total
SELECT soh.SalesOrderID, SUM(sod.LineTotal) AS OrderTotal
FROM Sales.SalesOrderHeader soh
JOIN Sales.SalesOrderDetail sod ON sod.SalesOrderID = soh.SalesOrderID
JOIN Sales.SpecialOfferProduct promo ON promo.ProductID = sod.ProductID
GROUP BY soh.SalesOrderID;

-- FIXED: order total computed in isolation, before any promotion join
WITH OrderTotals AS (
    SELECT soh.SalesOrderID, SUM(sod.LineTotal) AS OrderTotal
    FROM Sales.SalesOrderHeader soh
    JOIN Sales.SalesOrderDetail sod ON sod.SalesOrderID = soh.SalesOrderID
    GROUP BY soh.SalesOrderID
)
SELECT * FROM OrderTotals;
commonMistakes: Assuming a correct, relating join condition rules out row duplication entirely
Not comparing row counts (or a known-good total) before and after adding the third join
Reaching for SUM(DISTINCT ...) as a quick fix, which only coincidentally works and breaks again as soon as two genuinely different line totals happen to match
Combining two separate one-to-many expansions in one flat query feeding a single aggregate, instead of pre-aggregating each one to the grain actually needed
keyPoints: A correct join condition can still fan out rows when the relationship is genuinely one-to-many
Fan-out duplicates rows before aggregation runs, inflating any SUM downstream
This is distinct from a Cartesian product, which comes from a missing or non-relating join condition
Fix: pre-aggregate each one-to-many relationship to the needed grain in its own subquery/CTE before joining further

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses join fan-out (not a Cartesian product)
Explains why the duplication inflates the SUM
Proposes a correct fix (pre-aggregating before joining further)

questions.title: Two departments, two different 'official' numbers
questions.prompt: Finance and Marketing both publish a monthly 'Active Customers' count, and the two numbers have never matched. Each department insists its own number is correct. As someone newly tasked with fixing this, what's the root governance problem, and what's your first move?
questions.modelAnswer: The root problem is the absence of a single agreed-upon owner and definition for 'Active Customer' — each department built its own interpretation, with different time windows, different source systems, or different inclusion rules, and no shared, approved business glossary definition behind either one. This isn't primarily a technical bug; it's a governance gap. The first move isn't to pick a side technically — it's to bring both departments' stakeholders together, surface each one's actual definition and business rule in detail, and drive toward a single, approved, owned definition recorded in a business glossary that both then implement consistently.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd resist the urge to dive into either department's SQL first. Instead I'd set up a short working session with both sides, write down each department's actual definition side by side, and find the real difference -- maybe Finance counts a 12-month window and Marketing counts 6, or one includes trial accounts and the other doesn't. Once the real gap is visible, I'd escalate to whoever is the designated owner of the Customer domain to make the final call, then record that authoritative definition in a governed glossary entry, and redirect both reports to reference it going forward instead of their own private logic.
