Picking one department's number arbitrarily without stakeholder buy-in, which doesn't fix the underlying governance gap
Assuming this is purely a technical/data problem rather than a missing-ownership problem
Fixing the current discrepancy without creating an owned, documented definition, so the same conflict just recurs with the next new report
keyPoints: Conflicting numbers for the same term are usually a missing-ownership/definition problem, not a bug
The fix starts with surfacing and reconciling both actual definitions, not jumping to code
A designated owner needs to make and document the final call
The resolution should be recorded in a governed glossary entry so it doesn't recur

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the missing-ownership/definition root cause
Describes a sensible stakeholder-reconciliation first move
Proposes recording the resolution in a governed glossary entry

questions.title: High completeness score, still 'missing' data complaints
questions.prompt: A data quality dashboard reports 98% completeness on the Customer Phone column, but business users keep complaining they 'can't reach half their customers.' What's probably being missed, and what would you check next?
questions.modelAnswer: Completeness only confirms a value is present — it says nothing about whether that value is actually correct, current, or usable, which is what accuracy and validity cover. A phone field can be 98% 'filled in' while still being full of disconnected numbers, outdated numbers, or entries that are technically present but invalid, like placeholder values such as '000-000-0000.' The next check should look at validity — does the value actually match an expected phone format or pattern — and, where possible, accuracy — is the number still correct and reachable, which usually needs an external verification signal rather than just an internal profiling query.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd pull a sample of the 'complete' phone numbers and actually look at them, rather than trusting the single completeness score. I'd check for obvious junk or placeholder patterns, look at how long it's been since each record's phone field was last updated, and check whether a validity rule -- a format or pattern check -- was ever actually applied to this column at all. My guess going in is that a lot of those 98% 'filled in' values are either stale or placeholder junk that was entered just to satisfy a required-field rule somewhere upstream, which completeness alone can never catch.
commonMistakes: Treating a single high completeness score as proof the column is healthy, without checking other dimensions
Not sampling actual values to look for placeholder or junk data hiding behind a 'filled in' field
Assuming accuracy can be fully verified internally without any external confirmation signal
Never adding a validity rule or format check to catch junk entries going forward
keyPoints: Completeness measures presence only, not correctness or currency
A high completeness score can hide validity and accuracy problems
Validity checks (format/pattern rules) are the logical next thing to add
True accuracy often needs an external verification signal beyond what internal profiling can confirm

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the completeness-vs-accuracy/validity gap
Proposes a concrete next check (sampling, validity rule)
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: Two systems, two codes for the same status
questions.prompt: A CRM stores customer status as 'Active' / 'Inactive,' while the billing system stores the same concept as 'A' / 'I.' A report joining the two systems on status is silently dropping rows where the values don't line up. What data quality dimension does this fall under, and how would you fix it structurally rather than patching the one report?
questions.modelAnswer: This is a consistency problem — the same real-world concept is represented differently across systems, so values that mean the same thing don't match when compared or joined directly. Patching the single report, by hardcoding a CASE or mapping inline, fixes that one report but leaves the same mismatch waiting to break the next one. The structural fix is a documented, governed cross-system mapping or reference table — a status-code crosswalk maintained centrally — that every report or pipeline joining these systems uses, so the translation is defined once and reused everywhere instead of reinvented inconsistently report by report.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd build a small reference table -- SourceSystem, SourceCode, StandardStatus -- document it, and have both the CRM-facing and billing-facing pipelines reference it consistently going forward, rather than each report author inventing their own CASE statement. I'd also set it up so that any new, unmapped code shows up as a flagged exception rather than silently falling out of the join the way it is right now -- right now the data isn't 'wrong,' it's just represented two different ways, and the join is quietly dropping legitimate rows because nobody's telling it the two representations mean the same thing.
commonMistakes: Hardcoding a one-off CASE or mapping inside a single report instead of building a shared, reusable mapping
Not noticing rows are being silently dropped by the join at all, mistaking a mismatch for genuinely missing data
Assuming 'the data is wrong' rather than recognizing it's a representation-consistency problem across systems
Letting unmapped new codes fail silently instead of flagging them for review
keyPoints: This is a consistency dimension problem, not a completeness or accuracy one
A per-report patch doesn't fix the underlying mismatch for the next report
The structural fix is a shared, governed cross-system mapping or reference table
New unmapped values should be flagged, not silently dropped

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies this as a consistency problem
Proposes a structural fix (shared crosswalk) over a one-off patch
Mentions flagging unmapped values going forward

questions.title: An upstream rename breaks a downstream report with no warning
questions.prompt: A source system team renames a column from CustAmt to CustomerAmount as part of a cleanup, without telling anyone. Three weeks later, a downstream revenue report starts showing zeros, and nobody can explain why until someone manually traces the pipeline back to the source. What governance capability was missing here, and what would have prevented the three-week delay?
questions.modelAnswer: What's missing is documented lineage paired with an impact-analysis process tied to upstream changes — without a record of which downstream reports or tables actually depend on CustAmt, the source team had no way to know their rename would break anything, and the downstream team had no quick way to confirm the cause once something broke. With lineage documented, the source team could have run an impact analysis before the change — 'what depends on this column' — and either notified the downstream owners or coordinated the update; with lineage in place, the downstream team could also have traced the zeros back to the renamed column in minutes instead of weeks of manual digging.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd treat a change-impact-assessment step as standard practice before any schema change like this: before renaming anything, query the lineage or catalog for everything that depends on CustAmt, notify every owner on that list, and coordinate the change instead of just making it quietly. This specific incident -- three weeks of confusion over a renamed column -- is exactly the kind of case a basic upstream/downstream dependency map is built to prevent, and it's also exactly the kind of case that makes the investment in maintaining lineage obviously worth it the first time it actually saves someone three weeks.
commonMistakes: Making a source-side schema change without checking, or even knowing how to check, what depends on it downstream
Having no documented lineage at all, so tracing the breakage after the fact takes manual archaeology instead of a quick lookup
Treating a column rename as a purely internal, low-risk change instead of an input to a broader pipeline
Not establishing a change-notification process for data producers to follow before making breaking changes
keyPoints: This is a missing impact-analysis/dependency-mapping problem, not a data quality problem
Documented lineage lets you ask 'what depends on this' before making a change
Without lineage, root-causing a broken downstream report takes manual, slow tracing
A change-notification process for upstream producers prevents this class of incident

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies missing lineage/impact analysis as the root cause
Explains how impact analysis before the change would have helped
Explains how lineage would have sped up the after-the-fact investigation

questions.title: Two teams, two 'owners,' same metric
questions.prompt: Both the Finance team and the Marketing team claim ownership of the 'Customer Lifetime Value' (CLV) metric, and each has quietly built their own version with different assumptions. What's gone wrong from a governance-structure standpoint, and how should ownership actually be resolved here?
questions.modelAnswer: Ownership for a given data domain or metric should be singular and clearly assigned — when two teams each informally claim it, that's a sign governance never actually assigned, or enforced, a single accountable owner for CLV in the first place, so both teams filled the vacuum independently. Resolving it isn't about deciding whose formula happens to be more sophisticated; it's a governance decision. A governance council or executive sponsor should designate one accountable owner — likely whichever function the metric most directly serves, or a neutral shared analytics/governance function — who then becomes responsible for the single approved definition, with the other team becoming a consumer or a documented stakeholder providing input, not a second owner.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't try to referee this by comparing the two formulas line by line. I'd escalate it to a governance council or sponsor and frame it explicitly as an ownership decision that needs to be made and documented, not a technical dispute to be merged. Once a single owner is designated, I'd have them publish the one approved CLV definition in the business glossary, and the other team shifts to being a consumer of that definition -- still free to raise input or concerns, but no longer maintaining a separate, competing version. The part I'd insist on is documenting the decision, because an undocumented verbal resolution tends to quietly drift back into two versions within a year.
commonMistakes: Trying to resolve this technically by merging the two formulas instead of recognizing it's a missing-single-owner problem
Assuming whichever team built theirs first or more elaborately should automatically win
Resolving it informally between the two teams with no escalation path or documented decision
Not updating the glossary/dictionary afterward, letting the old duplicate definitions linger and get reused
keyPoints: A metric or domain should have exactly one accountable owner, not two informal ones
The fix is a governance decision made via a council or sponsor, not a technical merge of formulas
The non-owning team becomes a consumer/stakeholder, not a co-owner
The resolution must be documented in the glossary so it actually sticks

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the missing-single-owner governance gap
Proposes resolving it as a governance decision, not a technical merge
Mentions documenting the resolution to make it stick

questions.title: A glossary term that was never actually approved
questions.prompt: A data steward discovers that a business glossary term, 'Qualified Lead,' has been used in several reports for over a year — but it was entered by one analyst and never went through any review or approval. Two of the reports using it don't even agree on what it means. What process gap does this reveal, and how should it be fixed going forward?
questions.modelAnswer: The gap is a missing glossary governance and approval workflow — a term was published and relied on without ever being reviewed and formally approved by an accountable owner, so there was never a single authoritative version anyone had to conform to, which is exactly how two reports ended up quietly diverging. The fix is establishing, and actually enforcing, a review-and-approval step before any new glossary term is marked approved and usable: a designated reviewer or owner checks the definition for clarity and business accuracy, resolves ambiguity, and only then does the term become the authoritative reference reports are expected to use — with existing unreviewed terms like this one retroactively run through that same process.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd treat this as a retroactive audit as much as a go-forward fix. First, I'd pull every glossary term with no recorded approval -- 'Qualified Lead' almost certainly isn't the only one -- and route them all through a lightweight review process. For 'Qualified Lead' specifically, I'd bring the owners of the two conflicting reports together, have them agree on one actual definition, and only then republish the term as formally approved. Going forward, I'd make sure no new term can get published and relied on in a report without passing through that same review step, so this doesn't quietly happen again with the next ad hoc term someone adds.
commonMistakes: Letting any analyst publish a glossary term with no review step at all
Assuming a glossary entry existing for a long time means it must already be correct or approved
Not periodically auditing the glossary for terms lacking a recorded owner or approval
Fixing just this one term without addressing the broader missing approval workflow that let it happen
keyPoints: A glossary term should require review and approval by an accountable owner before being considered authoritative
Terms lacking this are exactly where conflicting usage quietly creeps in
The fix is both retroactive (audit existing unreviewed terms) and process-level (require approval going forward)
Conflicting usages discovered need to be reconciled into one approved definition, not just flagged

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the missing approval-workflow gap
Proposes a retroactive audit of unreviewed terms
Proposes a concrete go-forward approval process

questions.title: A revenue drop takes two days to explain because no one documented the pipeline
questions.prompt: Q3 revenue suddenly drops 15% on the executive dashboard. It takes an analyst two full days of asking around and reading old emails to figure out that a currency-conversion step was quietly changed upstream. What's the underlying problem, and what would you put in place so the next investigation like this takes minutes, not days?
questions.modelAnswer: The underlying problem is the absence of maintained lineage documentation — nobody had a readily available, trustworthy map of which systems, transformation steps, and business rules feed into the Q3 revenue figure, so investigating the drop meant manually reconstructing that knowledge from scattered memory and old emails instead of looking it up. The fix is documenting the full source-to-report lineage for this metric, and other high-priority critical metrics, up front — every source, every transformation step including business rules like currency conversion, and the load schedule — kept current as the pipeline changes, so the next time something looks off, the investigation starts with checking the documented lineage instead of asking around.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd build out a lineage diagram or document for the revenue metric specifically, and I'd make a point of calling out the currency-conversion step explicitly as a documented business rule, not just an implementation detail buried in code -- that's exactly the kind of step that's easy to change quietly and expensive to track down later, which is precisely what just happened. I'd also establish a habit of updating that documentation whenever that step actually changes, because a lineage doc that goes stale the first time someone tweaks the pipeline is barely better than having none at all.
commonMistakes: Relying on informal or tribal knowledge instead of documented lineage for a metric that matters this much
Not specifically calling out business-rule transformation steps, like currency conversion, in lineage documentation
Not updating lineage documentation when a pipeline step actually changes, letting it go stale and misleading
Treating this incident as a one-off rather than fixing the documentation gap that caused the slow investigation
keyPoints: Tribal-knowledge-only lineage leads to slow, manual investigations when something breaks
Documenting source-to-report lineage up front turns a two-day investigation into a quick lookup
Business-rule transformation steps, not just data movement, need to be explicitly documented
Lineage documentation needs to be kept current as the pipeline actually changes

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses missing/stale lineage documentation as the root cause
Proposes documenting business-rule steps explicitly, not just data movement
Mentions keeping documentation current as the pipeline changes

questions.title: Why Dev, QA, and Production stay separate
questions.prompt: Why does a BI team typically maintain separate Dev, QA, and Production SQL Server environments, and promote a change through them in that fixed order, instead of just building and testing directly against the Production database that live reports and real users already depend on?
questions.modelAnswer: Dev is where new work is actually built, and it's expected to be unstable -- half-finished packages, broken queries, and throwaway test data are all normal there, and critically, none of that instability is visible to anyone who depends on real numbers. QA is a separate, more stable environment with data that resembles Production, used specifically to verify a change behaves correctly before any real user is ever exposed to it -- this is where testing is supposed to happen, not in Dev and not in Production. Production is the environment real business users and live reports actually run against, and it's deliberately the last environment any change reaches, only after being built in Dev and then validated in QA. Testing directly against Production is risky for two concrete reasons: an in-progress or buggy change can lock, corrupt, or simply show wrong numbers in data that live reports depend on right now, and there's no safe way to test something genuinely risky -- a schema change, a large bulk load -- without potentially causing a real outage if it goes wrong. Promoting a change through Dev, then QA, then Production in that fixed order guarantees every change gets at least one chance to fail somewhere that doesn't matter yet before it ever reaches somewhere that does.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame it around what's allowed to break where. Dev is allowed to break -- that's the whole point of it, it's where I'm actively building and nobody real is looking at it. QA is where I prove a change actually works against data that looks like the real thing, before any real user sees it. Production is the one environment where breaking something has an actual business cost, so it's deliberately the last stop, not the first. If I skipped straight to testing in Production, the two real risks are: a change that's still buggy could corrupt or lock data that a live report is reading from right now, and there's no safe way to rehearse something genuinely risky, like a schema change, without actually risking the outage I was trying to avoid. The fixed Dev-then-QA-then-Production order is really just making sure every change gets tested somewhere low-stakes before it reaches somewhere high-stakes.
commonMistakes: Making a direct change in Production 'just this once' to save time
Treating QA as optional for a change that 'seems small' instead of validating it there first
Letting QA's data drift so far from Production's that it stops catching real issues
Conflating Dev and QA as the same environment instead of recognizing their different purposes (building vs. validating)
keyPoints: Dev is for building and is expected to be unstable, isolated from real users
QA validates a change against production-like data before any real user is exposed to it
Production is the last environment reached, only after Dev and QA
Direct Production changes risk live data and can't safely rehearse risky operations

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes the purpose of each environment (Dev, QA, Production)
Correctly explains the risk of testing directly in Production
Explains why the promotion order matters

questions.title: Why use a framework like DAMA-DMBOK instead of inventing your own
questions.prompt: What is DAMA-DMBOK, at a high level, and why would an organization starting a governance program benefit from adopting an established framework rather than designing its own governance structure entirely from scratch?
questions.modelAnswer: DAMA-DMBOK -- the Data Management Body of Knowledge, published by DAMA International -- is a widely recognized reference framework that defines the knowledge areas of data management, including governance, quality, and metadata, along with common terminology, roles, and practices. Adopting it, or a similar established framework, gives a new program a tested starting structure and shared vocabulary instead of inventing one from zero, which matters especially because governance success depends heavily on getting different departments to speak the same language about data -- a homegrown framework risks reinventing definitions and roles that already have well-understood industry equivalents, slowing adoption and making it harder to hire or train people into a structure no one outside the organization recognizes.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd compare a DAMA-aligned role structure -- data owner, data steward, data custodian -- against a homegrown one invented from scratch. If I use the established terms, a new hire who's worked in governance elsewhere already roughly understands what a 'data steward' does on day one. If I invent my own terminology and structure instead, I'm spending time training everyone on vocabulary that only means something inside this one organization, with no outside reference to lean on. I wouldn't adopt DAMA-DMBOK wholesale without adapting it, though -- the framework is broad enough to cover a huge range of maturity levels, so part of the job is picking the pieces that actually fit the organization's current size and needs rather than building out every knowledge area at once.
commonMistakes: Adopting DAMA-DMBOK wholesale without adapting it to the organization's actual size or maturity, producing an overbuilt program
Assuming a framework alone constitutes a governance program, when it still needs real people, process, and executive sponsorship
Dismissing frameworks entirely and reinventing basic terminology or structure that already has a well-understood standard
Treating the framework as rigid rules to follow exactly rather than a reference to adapt
keyPoints: DAMA-DMBOK is an established reference framework covering governance, quality, metadata, and other data management knowledge areas
Using an established framework provides shared vocabulary and a tested starting structure
Frameworks need to be adapted to the organization's actual size and maturity, not adopted rigidly
A framework alone isn't a program -- it still needs real people, process, and sponsorship behind it

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes what DAMA-DMBOK is
Explains the benefit of shared vocabulary/structure over a homegrown approach
Notes the need to adapt a framework rather than adopt it rigidly

questions.title: Centralized vs. federated governance operating models
questions.prompt: What's the practical difference between a centralized, a decentralized, and a federated data governance operating model? Why do most organizations end up somewhere closer to federated rather than purely one or the other?
questions.modelAnswer: Centralized means a single, central team makes governance decisions and sets policy for the entire organization -- consistent, but can be slow and disconnected from the realities of individual business units. Decentralized means each business unit or domain governs its own data independently, with no central coordination -- fast and locally relevant, but prone to inconsistent definitions and duplicated effort across units, the same 'two departments, two numbers' problem that comes from no shared authority. Federated is a hybrid: a central body sets organization-wide standards, shared policy, and common tooling, while individual business domains retain day-to-day ownership and stewardship within that shared framework. Most organizations land near federated because it balances consistency -- avoiding the decentralized model's fragmentation -- with practicality and speed -- avoiding the centralized model's bottleneck and disconnect from domain expertise.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe a federated setup concretely: a central governance office defines the glossary-approval process and naming standards that apply everywhere, while individual domain stewards in Sales or Finance actually define and maintain their own domain's specific terms within that shared process. That's the balance most organizations end up wanting -- enough central structure that Sales and Finance aren't inventing incompatible processes from scratch, but enough local ownership that the people closest to the data are the ones actually maintaining it day to day. The part I'd flag as easy to get wrong is leaving the boundary fuzzy -- a federated model only works if it's clear exactly which decisions are central and which are left to the domain; blur that line and you end up with the worst of both models instead of the best.
commonMistakes: Assuming one model is universally correct instead of recognizing the tradeoff each one makes
Implementing a purely centralized model in a large, diverse organization and creating a bottleneck
Implementing a purely decentralized model and being surprised when definitions conflict across units
Leaving the central-vs-local boundary ambiguous in a federated model, which defeats the point of federating
keyPoints: Centralized = central authority, consistent but slow and potentially disconnected
Decentralized = local autonomy, fast but fragmented and inconsistent
Federated = central standards plus local ownership within them, a common middle ground
A federated model still needs clear boundaries on what's central versus local decision-making

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines all three operating models
Explains the tradeoff each model makes
Explains why federated is the common middle ground

questions.title: Why governance programs start with a council, not a tool
questions.prompt: A new data governance program is about to kick off. Why would establishing a governance council or committee typically come before selecting and rolling out a governance tool (a catalog, a glossary platform, etc.)?
questions.modelAnswer: A tool only executes decisions -- it doesn't make them. Without a governance council -- the group of accountable stakeholders who actually have the authority to set policy, approve definitions, resolve disputes between domains, and assign owners -- there's no one empowered to decide what the tool should even enforce or contain, so rolling out a catalog or glossary platform first typically produces an empty or inconsistently-populated tool that nobody is accountable for keeping accurate. Standing up the council first establishes who's accountable for governance decisions, giving the later tool rollout actual substance -- approved definitions, assigned owners, agreed policies -- to populate and enforce, rather than an expensive piece of software with no real governance behind it.
questions.professionalAnswer: I've seen the cautionary version of this play out: buy a catalog tool, auto-import every table in the warehouse, and end up with thousands of undocumented, unowned entries because there was no council yet to actually assign ownership or approve any definitions. I'd rather stand up the council first, get a handful of critical data elements properly owned and defined through an actual working process, and only then roll out tooling to scale something that's already proven to work on a small scale. The tool's workflow and approval features are useful, but they're only useful once there are real empowered people behind them making the calls.
commonMistakes: Rolling out a governance tool before any accountable group exists to feed it real decisions, producing an empty or stale tool
Assuming a tool's features, like workflow or approval steps, substitute for actually having empowered people behind them
Skipping the step of defining who sits on the council and what authority they actually have
Treating council formation as a formality instead of the actual seat of governance decision-making
keyPoints: A council or committee is where governance decisions and accountability actually live
A tool only executes and enforces decisions, it doesn't make them
Rolling out a tool before a council exists usually produces an empty or unowned result
Council-first lets the eventual tool rollout scale an already-working decision process

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why a council precedes a tool

questions.title: How a data quality program's pieces fit together end to end
questions.prompt: A data quality program typically includes profiling, rules/checks, remediation, and monitoring. At a high level, how do these four pieces fit together as one ongoing cycle, rather than four unrelated activities?
questions.modelAnswer: Profiling comes first -- examining the actual data's distributions, nulls, and patterns to understand its current state and surface likely problems before deciding what to check. Rules and checks are built based on what profiling revealed and what the business cares about, turning informal observations into specific, automatable pass/fail tests, like completeness thresholds, format validation, or referential checks. When a check fails, remediation is the actual work of fixing the underlying bad data, or the process that produced it, rather than just flagging it and moving on. Monitoring then runs the same checks on an ongoing, automated basis so new issues are caught quickly after they're introduced rather than being rediscovered from scratch -- and what monitoring surfaces often feeds back into re-profiling as the data or business rules evolve, making this a continuous cycle rather than a one-time project.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through this as a loop on a concrete example. I'd profile a Customer table and discover the phone-number format is a mess. That observation turns into a validity rule -- does the value match an expected phone pattern -- which flags every violation. I'd remediate the worst offenders by actually cleaning up the data, not just noting that it's bad. Then I'd schedule that same validity check to run nightly going forward as ongoing monitoring, specifically so new bad records get caught quickly instead of silently piling back up the way they did before anyone looked. And if monitoring later shows the rule itself needs adjusting -- maybe a new valid format shows up -- that sends me back to re-profile and refine the rule, which is exactly why this is a cycle, not a project with a defined end.
commonMistakes: Treating profiling as a one-time kickoff activity instead of something to revisit as data evolves
Writing rules or checks without first profiling, guessing at thresholds instead of basing them on the data's actual observed state
Detecting failures through monitoring but never actually remediating the underlying issue, letting flagged problems pile up
Building checks and remediation but skipping ongoing monitoring, so the same issues quietly recur after the initial cleanup
keyPoints: Profiling examines actual data to inform what checks are worth building
Rules and checks turn observations into automatable, testable conditions
Remediation is the real fix, not just flagging
Monitoring runs checks continuously and feeds back into re-profiling, making this a cycle, not a one-time project

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains each of the four pieces
Explains how they connect as an ongoing cycle, not isolated steps
Uses a concrete example to illustrate the cycle

questions.title: Why keep metadata in one central repository instead of per-team spreadsheets
questions.prompt: Why do governance programs push for a central metadata repository instead of letting each team keep its own spreadsheet or document describing its own tables and terms?
questions.modelAnswer: A metadata repository is a shared, structured, searchable store of metadata -- business glossary terms, data dictionary entries, ownership, lineage -- that everyone in the organization can look up, as opposed to scattered per-team spreadsheets, which inevitably drift apart, go stale, duplicate effort across teams, and are invisible to anyone outside that specific team. Centralizing metadata in one repository means a term or table only needs to be documented once, findable by anyone who needs it, which supports reuse and consistency, and it becomes the place where ownership, approval status, and relationships between terms, tables, and lineage can actually be tracked and enforced -- none of which a disconnected set of spreadsheets can reliably do at scale.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe the failure mode directly, because it's what actually drives the push for centralization: Team A's spreadsheet defines 'Active Customer' one way, Team B's spreadsheet defines it slightly differently, and neither team even knows the other spreadsheet exists until two conflicting reports collide. A central repository doesn't automatically prevent that disagreement from happening, but it at least makes the conflict visible and searchable instead of hidden in two separate files nobody else can see. I'd also point out that centralizing metadata is as much a process change as a tooling one -- the repository still needs the same ownership and review rigor a good spreadsheet-based approach would also need; a central tool with sloppy content isn't actually better than a well-maintained spreadsheet.
commonMistakes: Assuming a spreadsheet is 'good enough' for a small team without considering how metadata needs scale as more teams and reports depend on the same data
Letting duplicate, conflicting definitions persist invisibly across separate team documents
Not giving the central repository the same rigor (ownership, approval, review) that would also be needed in any decentralized approach
Treating centralization purely as a tooling choice instead of also a process and governance one
keyPoints: A central metadata repository is shared, structured, and searchable across the whole organization
Scattered team-level spreadsheets drift apart, duplicate effort, and hide conflicts instead of surfacing them
Centralizing metadata supports reuse, consistency, and tracking ownership/approval at scale
Centralization is a process change, not just a tooling change

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what a metadata repository provides
Correctly explains the failure modes of scattered spreadsheets
Notes that centralization also requires process rigor, not just a tool

questions.title: How the glossary, dictionary, and catalog fit together as layers
questions.prompt: How do a business glossary, a data dictionary, and a data catalog relate to each other architecturally? If someone asks 'where does the Active Customer count actually live in our systems,' which of the three would they start with, and which would eventually get them to the actual table?
questions.modelAnswer: Think of them as three layers serving different questions. The business glossary answers 'what does this term mean' in plain business language -- Active Customer is a customer with a purchase in the trailing 12 months. The data dictionary answers 'what's the actual technical structure' for a specific table or column -- the IsActiveFlag bit column in the Customer table. The data catalog is the searchable index that ties everything together and makes it discoverable, letting someone search 'Active Customer' and actually find the glossary definition and the specific dictionary-documented column(s) that implement it, across potentially many systems. Someone asking that question would typically start at the catalog, which surfaces the glossary definition for context and links through to the dictionary entry or entries for the actual physical location.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through a realistic search: open the catalog, search 'Active Customer,' and land on the approved glossary definition plus a linked data dictionary entry showing exactly which table and column in which system implements it -- possibly across two systems if more than one source counts toward the metric. The catalog itself doesn't generate good content on its own, though; it's an index over glossary and dictionary content that still has to be authored, reviewed, and kept current -- a catalog pointing at thin or missing glossary and dictionary entries isn't much more useful than no catalog at all.
commonMistakes: Treating the three as redundant or interchangeable instead of serving distinct questions (meaning vs. structure vs. discoverability)
Building a dictionary or glossary with no catalog tying them together, leaving them undiscoverable to anyone who doesn't already know where to look
Assuming a catalog automatically creates good glossary or dictionary content on its own, when it's really an index over content that still has to be authored and maintained
Not linking glossary terms to their underlying technical implementation, leaving a nice definition with no path to the actual data
keyPoints: Glossary = business meaning
Dictionary = technical structure
Catalog = searchable index linking the two and making them discoverable
A catalog without well-maintained glossary/dictionary content underneath it has little real value

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines the role of each of the three layers
Correctly applies the layers to the Active Customer example
Notes that a catalog depends on well-maintained content underneath it

questions.title: Business, technical, and operational metadata as three distinct layers
questions.prompt: What's the difference between business metadata, technical metadata, and operational metadata? Give one example of each for the same table.
questions.modelAnswer: Business metadata describes meaning in business terms -- the glossary definition, the business owner, the business rule behind a field. Technical metadata describes the physical and structural facts about the data object itself -- column names, data types, constraints, indexes. Operational metadata describes how the data actually moves and behaves at runtime -- when a table was last loaded, how long the load took, row counts, job success or failure history. For a single Orders table: business metadata might be 'Orders represents confirmed customer purchases, owned by the Sales domain'; technical metadata might be 'OrderID is an INT, primary key, NOT NULL'; operational metadata might be 'last successful load: 2026-10-08 02:14 AM, 42,311 rows loaded, duration 6 minutes.' Each answers a different question, and a mature metadata program captures all three, not just the technical layer most tools default to.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd point out that a lot of tools capture technical metadata easily, since it's sitting right there in the schema, and operational metadata reasonably easily too, since it's usually in job logs already. Business metadata is the one that almost always requires deliberate human effort -- someone has to actually write and get the definition and ownership approved -- which is exactly why it's so often the thinnest layer even when a catalog looks otherwise well-populated with technical detail. I'd treat operational metadata as more than a nice-to-have, too -- tracking load times and row counts over time is often the earliest warning sign that something upstream is quietly degrading, before anyone notices the actual numbers look wrong.
commonMistakes: Treating 'metadata' as only the technical/schema layer and ignoring business and operational metadata entirely
Assuming business metadata will get captured automatically by a tool the way technical metadata often does
Not tracking operational metadata (load times, row counts, failures), losing an early warning signal for pipeline problems
Conflating technical and operational metadata (structure vs. runtime behavior) as the same thing
keyPoints: Business metadata = meaning, ownership, and rules
Technical metadata = structure (types, constraints)
Operational metadata = runtime behavior (load times, row counts, job history)
Business metadata is the layer requiring the most deliberate human effort and is often the thinnest in practice

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes all three metadata types
Gives a correct example of each for the same table
Notes which layer tends to be thinnest in practice and why

questions.title: Business lineage vs. technical lineage — different audiences, different views
questions.prompt: What's the difference between business lineage and technical lineage, and why would a governance program maintain both instead of just the detailed technical version?
questions.modelAnswer: Technical lineage is the detailed, system-level trace of exactly how data physically moves -- specific tables, columns, jobs, scripts, and transformation logic -- useful to engineers debugging a pipeline. Business lineage is a higher-level, plain-language view of the same journey, described in terms business stakeholders actually understand -- which source systems and business processes feed a given report, without requiring knowledge of specific table or column names. A program needs both because they serve different audiences and questions: an executive or auditor asking 'where does this number ultimately come from, in terms I understand' needs business lineage, while an engineer asking 'which specific job and transformation step is actually broken' needs the technical detail -- showing only the technical version to a non-technical stakeholder overwhelms them with irrelevant detail, while showing only the business version to an engineer leaves out exactly what they need to actually fix something.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe both views of the same revenue pipeline side by side. Business lineage says: Sales Orders feeds the Revenue Recognition Process, which feeds Finance Reporting -- that's the version I'd show an auditor or an executive. Technical lineage says: OrderEntry's Orders table feeds an ETL job, which loads a warehouse fact table, which a semantic model turns into a TotalRevenue measure -- that's the version an engineer actually needs to go fix something. It's the same real journey described at two different levels of detail, and I wouldn't assume one can just be generated automatically from the other -- the business-level version usually needs a deliberate simplification step, written for a non-technical reader on purpose.
commonMistakes: Maintaining only technical lineage and expecting business stakeholders to interpret it themselves
Maintaining only a business-level summary with no technical detail, leaving engineers with nothing to actually debug
Assuming one view can simply be generated from the other with no additional work, when business lineage usually needs a deliberate simplification/translation step
Not keeping both versions in sync as the pipeline changes
keyPoints: Technical lineage = detailed, system-level trace for engineers
Business lineage = plain-language, process-level view for business stakeholders and auditors
Both serve the same underlying journey but answer different audiences' questions
Maintaining only one leaves a real audience without what they actually need

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes business lineage from technical lineage
Explains why both are needed, with correct audience examples
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: Why column-level lineage matters more once you actually need impact analysis
questions.prompt: What's the difference between table-level lineage and column-level lineage? If a specific column is about to be dropped from a source table, which level of lineage actually tells you whether it's safe to do, and why doesn't the other level answer that question well?
questions.modelAnswer: Table-level lineage shows that data flows from Table A into Table B, and onward, without specifying which individual columns were actually used in that flow. Column-level lineage tracks that same flow down to the individual field -- which specific source column fed which specific target column, through which transformation. If a specific column is about to be dropped, table-level lineage can only tell you that Table A feeds into some downstream tables generally -- it can't tell you whether this particular column is actually used by any of them, so it could falsely suggest wide impact, with everything touching Table A looking 'at risk,' or miss real impact entirely if dependency tracking is too coarse. Column-level lineage is what actually answers 'is it safe to drop this column' precisely, by showing exactly which downstream columns or reports genuinely depend on it, rather than an undifferentiated table-to-table relationship.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe a near-miss to make the point concrete: table-level lineage suggested a column was safe to drop because nothing important seemed to depend on the table it belonged to in any critical way. Column-level lineage told a different story -- that specific column quietly fed a measure in an executive dashboard that the table-level view had no way of surfacing, because it only tracks table-to-table flow, not field-to-field. I don't build column-level lineage everywhere, though, since it takes real extra effort to construct and maintain -- I'd prioritize it specifically for critical data elements, where that extra precision is actually worth the cost.
commonMistakes: Relying on table-level lineage alone to judge whether a specific column change is safe
Assuming table-level lineage is 'basically the same thing, just less detailed,' when for column-specific impact questions it isn't a safe substitute
Underestimating how much more effort column-level lineage takes to build and maintain, and so skipping it even for genuinely high-risk critical data elements
Not maintaining column-level lineage specifically for CDEs where the extra precision actually matters most
keyPoints: Table-level lineage shows flow between tables without specifying which columns are involved
Column-level lineage tracks the field-to-field relationship precisely
Only column-level lineage reliably answers 'is this specific column safe to change or drop'
The extra effort of column-level lineage is most worth investing in for critical data elements

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes table-level from column-level lineage
Correctly explains why only column-level lineage answers the drop-safety question
Notes the cost tradeoff and where to prioritize column-level lineage

questions.title: What you'd say in your first stand-up
questions.prompt: What is a Daily Scrum (stand-up), and what would you actually say during one in your first week on a new BI team?
questions.modelAnswer: A Daily Scrum, commonly called a stand-up, is a short, time-boxed daily meeting -- often 15 minutes -- where the team synchronizes with itself on progress and blockers; it's explicitly not a status report delivered upward to a manager, it's the team talking to each other. The typical shape each person covers is roughly: what I did since the last stand-up, what I'm doing until the next one, and anything blocking me. A strong first-week answer from a junior team member stays specific and brief rather than vague: naming the actual ticket or task worked on, being honest and specific about being stuck rather than saying a vague 'I'm still working on it,' and flagging a blocker the moment it's identified rather than waiting to mention it, since the whole point of surfacing a blocker in stand-up is getting help from the team quickly, not saving face. A junior new hire should resist the urge to over-explain or justify slow progress at length -- stand-up is meant to be short, and a longer conversation about a specific blocker belongs in a follow-up afterward, not consuming the whole meeting.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd keep it short and specific, something like: 'Yesterday I finished writing the Lookup for the Customer dimension and started on the fact table load. Today I'm wiring up the error output so bad rows get redirected instead of failing the whole package. I'm blocked on getting read access to the QA staging database, so if anyone can help with that after stand-up, I'd appreciate it.' That covers all three parts -- what I did, what I'm doing, what's blocking me -- in under thirty seconds, and it names a real ticket instead of a vague status. I'd also remind myself that stand-up isn't the place to actually solve the blocker; it's the place to surface it so the right person can grab me right after.
commonMistakes: Treating stand-up like a status report to a manager instead of the team syncing with itself
Being vague ('still working on it') instead of naming the specific ticket or task
Saving a blocker until later instead of surfacing it the moment it's identified
Turning stand-up into a long problem-solving discussion instead of flagging it briefly and following up afterward
keyPoints: Daily Scrum/stand-up is short, time-boxed, and team-to-team, not a report to a manager
Typical shape: what I did, what I'm doing next, what's blocking me
Name specific work, not vague progress statements
Surface blockers immediately; save detailed discussion for after stand-up

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes what a stand-up is and its purpose
Gives a specific, well-structured example of what to say
Avoids the common vague-status-report trap

questions.title: Recognizing 'blocked' vs. just behind
questions.prompt: You've been working on a ticket and progress has stalled. How do you tell whether you're just behind schedule or genuinely blocked, and how do you communicate that to your team?
questions.modelAnswer: 'Off Track' means the work is simply taking longer than planned -- normal, and usually just needs more time or a closer look, with progress still genuinely possible on your own. 'Blocked' means the work has hit a hard stop entirely outside your control -- a pending approval, a broken test environment, a dependency on another team -- where no amount of your own effort moves it forward until that's resolved. The practical test is asking: is there anything I can still personally do right now to make progress on this? If yes, it's Off Track -- keep working and simply mention in stand-up that it's taking longer than expected. If no -- you're waiting on someone or something outside your control -- it's Blocked, and it should be flagged clearly and immediately, not saved for the next scheduled meeting, since every day a real blocker goes unflagged is a day of work not getting unstuck sooner.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd ask myself one question: is there anything I can actually still do myself, right now, to move this forward? If the honest answer is yes -- I just need more time, or I need to think through the approach again -- that's Off Track, and I'd keep grinding and just flag in stand-up that it's taking longer than I estimated. If the honest answer is no -- I'm waiting on an approval, a broken environment, or someone on another team -- that's genuinely Blocked, and I wouldn't sit on it until the next stand-up. I'd flag it the moment I realize it, specifically naming what I actually need to get unblocked, rather than just saying 'I'm stuck,' because a specific ask is what actually gets someone to act on it quickly.
commonMistakes: Quietly grinding on a ticket without flagging it, assuming asking for help makes you look unprepared
Mislabeling 'off track' (just taking longer) as 'blocked' when there's still personal progress possible
Waiting until the next stand-up to mention a blocker instead of flagging it the moment it's identified
Flagging a blocker vaguely instead of saying specifically what's needed to unblock it
keyPoints: Off Track: work is simply taking longer than planned, more time/closer look resolves it
Blocked: a hard stop entirely outside your control -- no amount of personal effort moves it forward
The test: is there anything I can still do myself right now? If no, you're blocked
Flag a blocker immediately and specifically, not quietly or vaguely

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes Off Track from Blocked
Gives a usable decision test for telling them apart
Describes a clear, prompt way to communicate a real blocker

questions.title: Explaining why the team works in sprints, not all at once
questions.prompt: A stakeholder asks why your team can't just build the whole report and show it to them when it's completely done, instead of working in two-week sprints. How would you explain the difference between Agile and Waterfall to them, and why your team works the way it does?
questions.modelAnswer: Waterfall fits work where the requirements are genuinely stable and fully understood up front, moving through fixed phases once in order -- but if a requirement turns out to be wrong, that's usually not discovered until most of the work is already built, which makes it expensive to fix at that point. Agile instead breaks the same work into short, repeating two-week cycles, each one producing something real and working that the stakeholder can actually see and react to. The explanation should connect directly to the stakeholder's own interest rather than staying abstract: working in sprints means they get to say 'that's not quite what I meant' after two weeks of effort instead of after two months, which protects them, not just the team. It's also worth clarifying that a sprint still produces a genuinely working, shippable piece of the report each cycle -- not an unfinished fragment -- so showing it early isn't showing something broken.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd skip straight to what's in it for them. If we built the whole thing in one long pass and only showed it at the end, and it turned out we misunderstood something on day one, we wouldn't find that out until the entire report was already built -- which is expensive and slow to fix at that point. Working in two-week sprints means every two weeks you get to look at something real and tell us if we're headed the wrong direction, while that's still cheap to correct. I'd also be clear that what you're seeing every two weeks isn't a half-finished mess -- it's a genuinely working slice of the report, just not the whole thing yet. That's really the whole point of sprints: catching a misunderstanding in week two instead of week eight.
commonMistakes: Explaining Agile/Waterfall in the abstract without connecting it to why it benefits this stakeholder specifically
Implying sprints mean nothing gets fully finished, instead of explaining a sprint still produces a real, shippable increment
Being dismissive of the stakeholder's preference instead of explaining the real trade-off
Using unexplained jargon (backlog, increment, retrospective) instead of plain language
keyPoints: Waterfall fits stable, well-understood requirements but surfaces mistakes late and expensively
Agile's short cycles let the stakeholder react to real progress every 1-2 weeks, catching misunderstandings early
Connect the explanation to the stakeholder's own interest, not an abstract process lecture
Each sprint still produces a real, working increment, not an unfinished fragment

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Accurately explains the Agile vs. Waterfall trade-off
Connects the explanation to the stakeholder's own interest
Communicates without unexplained jargon

questions.title: Communicating during a live production incident
questions.prompt: Two days after a dashboard launches, a regional manager reports it's showing zero sales for their region all month. Walk me through how you'd investigate, and what you would communicate to the manager while you're still figuring out the cause.
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer separates the two parts of this question clearly. On investigation: start with the simplest explanation before anything complex -- did the dashboard's scheduled refresh actually run last night at all -- then work backward from the visible symptom toward the source, checking whether the ETL load completed for that region, whether the issue is in the underlying data or just a report-level filter, rather than guessing at a cause. On communication: send an honest, specific acknowledgment quickly -- confirming the report was received, that it's being looked into, and giving a concrete time to expect an update -- rather than staying silent until a fix is confirmed. It's expected and professional to communicate while still investigating, not only once the cause is found; silence during that window reads as neglect even when real work is happening behind the scenes.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd split this into what I say and what I actually do, and do the communication part first. Within a few minutes I'd send something like: 'Thanks for flagging this -- I'm looking into it now and will have an update for you by end of day.' That costs me almost nothing and tells the manager they haven't been forgotten. Then I'd investigate from the simplest explanation outward: did last night's scheduled refresh actually complete, or did it fail silently? If the refresh ran fine, I'd check whether that region's rows actually loaded into the fact table for this month, or whether this is a filter or slicer issue purely inside the report itself. I'd keep narrowing from the visible symptom back toward the source rather than guessing at something exotic first. Once I actually find the cause, I'd follow up with a clear explanation of what happened and what I changed -- not just a silent fix with no note at all.
commonMistakes: Staying silent until the fix is confirmed instead of acknowledging the report and giving a timeframe while still investigating
Jumping straight to a complex theory instead of checking the simplest thing first (did the scheduled refresh even run)
Investigating only inside the report itself without checking whether the issue actually originates further upstream in the data pipeline
Not giving the manager a concrete time to expect an update, leaving them to wonder if it's been forgotten
keyPoints: Communicate an acknowledgment and a timeframe immediately, don't wait for the fix to say anything
Investigate by narrowing from the visible symptom back toward the source (refresh status, pipeline, source data)
Check the simplest explanation first (did the scheduled load actually run) before assuming something complex
Follow up with a clear explanation once the cause is found, not just a silent fix

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes a logical investigation approach, working from symptom back to source
Correctly emphasizes communicating early, before the cause is known
Clarity and professionalism of the communication described

questions.title: Turning a vague business request into a user story
questions.prompt: A sales director emails you: 'Our regional managers keep asking me for last month's numbers by email. I need a dashboard that shows revenue by region and by product category, updated automatically, so they can check it themselves.' How would you turn that into a proper user story with acceptance criteria before you start building anything?
questions.modelAnswer: A user story is written from the user's point of view, in the shape 'As a [role], I want [capability], so that [benefit]' -- for this request: 'As a regional manager, I want a dashboard showing revenue by region and product category, so that I can check my own numbers without emailing the sales director.' A story alone is too vague to know when it's actually done, which is what acceptance criteria are for -- specific, checkable conditions, such as 'the dashboard reflects the prior day's closed sales by 7 AM each morning, with no manual steps' and 'the region filter defaults to the viewer's assigned territory.' Just as important is noticing what the original email left out: it never says what should happen when a region has zero sales for the month. A strong answer explicitly surfaces that gap -- either asking the sales director directly, or documenting a reasonable judgment call as its own acceptance criterion -- rather than silently guessing and discovering the wrong assumption after the dashboard is already built.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't start building from that email directly -- I'd turn it into a story first: 'As a regional manager, I want a dashboard showing revenue by region and product category, so that I can check my own numbers without emailing the sales director.' Then I'd write acceptance criteria that are actually checkable, not just a vague sense of done -- something like 'reflects yesterday's closed sales by 7 AM with no manual steps' and 'the region filter defaults to the viewer's own territory.' The thing I'd specifically flag before writing a single line of DAX is that the email never says what should happen if a region had zero sales that month -- show it as zero, blank, or leave it off the list entirely? I'd either ask the sales director directly or write down my own reasonable assumption as an explicit acceptance criterion, because guessing silently on that detail is exactly the kind of thing that comes back wrong during UAT.
commonMistakes: Starting to build directly from the vague email instead of writing a structured user story first
Writing a user story with no acceptance criteria, leaving 'done' undefined
Silently guessing at an ambiguous detail (like the zero-sales case) instead of asking or explicitly documenting the judgment call
Writing acceptance criteria that aren't actually checkable ('looks good') instead of specific and testable
keyPoints: User story shape: As a [role], I want [capability], so that [benefit]
Acceptance criteria must be specific and checkable, not vague
Explicitly surface and resolve ambiguous details (like the zero-sales edge case) before building
A story isn't ready to build until its acceptance criteria are defined

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Writes a correctly-shaped user story
Writes specific, checkable acceptance criteria
Identifies and resolves an ambiguous detail from the original request

questions.title: Asking for help when you're stuck
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time early in a project when you didn't know how to do something and had to ask a teammate or a more senior developer for help. How did you approach that conversation, and what did you do with the answer afterward?
questions.modelAnswer: This is a behavioral question testing resourcefulness and whether a candidate can ask for help effectively, rather than either staying silently stuck or outsourcing the thinking entirely to someone else. A strong answer shows an attempt was made first -- checking documentation, trying an approach, forming a specific theory -- since teams value someone who tries before asking, but it should also show the candidate didn't stay stuck in silence for an unreasonably long time out of fear of looking unprepared. When actually asking, the question should be specific -- naming what was tried and exactly where it broke down -- rather than a vague 'it's not working,' since a specific question gets a faster and more useful answer. The Action should also cover what happened after getting the answer: not just copying the fix, but understanding why it worked, so the same category of problem doesn't require asking again. Result should state a concrete outcome using STAR -- being unblocked within some stated timeframe, and ideally applying the same concept independently on a later, similar problem.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell one specific story. Situation: early in my capstone, I couldn't get an OLE DB Destination's fast-load mode to actually speed anything up, and I'd already tried switching the data access mode and rereading the component's tooltips with no luck. Task: I needed to actually understand what I was missing, not just make the error go away. Action: I asked a more experienced developer a specific question -- 'I switched to fast load, but it's still inserting one row at a time based on the execution time, here's what I've already tried' -- rather than just saying it wasn't working. They pointed out I still had the destination's table lock option unchecked, which was serializing the insert behind other activity on the table. Result: once I checked that option, the load time dropped noticeably, and I started checking that same setting by default on every OLE DB Destination I've built since, without needing to ask again. I'd keep the story specific and make sure it lands on that last point -- what I actually learned to do differently afterward.
commonMistakes: Staying stuck in silence for too long before asking, out of fear of looking unprepared
Asking a vague question ('it's not working') instead of naming what was tried and exactly where it broke down
Copying the fix without understanding why it worked, so the same type of problem requires asking again later
Describing a general attitude toward asking for help instead of telling one specific, real story with a stated Result
keyPoints: Show an attempt was made before asking, but don't stay stuck in silence too long either
Ask a specific question naming what was tried and where it broke down
Understand why the answer worked rather than just copying it
Use STAR and state a concrete Result, including what changed afterward

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Shows a reasonable attempt was made before asking for help
Tells a specific, real story using STAR
States a concrete Result, including what was learned or applied afterward

questions.title: Why move from Data Analyst toward BI Engineering
questions.prompt: You've been working as a Data Analyst. What's actually motivating you to grow into a BI Engineer role, and what have you been doing to build toward that?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer is specific about what actually changes between the two roles, not just a vague sense that BI Engineer 'sounds like a step up.' A Data Analyst typically works with data and models that already exist, answering business questions and building reports against them; a BI Engineer takes more ownership further upstream -- designing the data model itself, building and maintaining the pipelines and transformations that feed it, and being responsible for a report's reliability and performance, not just its content. A credible motivation names a specific experience that revealed that gap -- for example, repeatedly hitting the limits of what could be fixed inside a single report because the underlying model or data pipeline itself needed to change, and wanting to be the person who can make that change rather than only ever filing a request for someone else to make it. The second half of the answer should show concrete action already taken, not just intention -- specific skills being built (SQL beyond basic querying, data modeling, understanding how data gets from source systems into the model in the first place) rather than a general statement of enthusiasm.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd be specific rather than giving the generic 'I want to grow' answer. What actually pushed me toward this was hitting a point, a few times, where a report had a real problem -- slow, or a number that was technically right but the model structure made it clunky to get at -- and the fix wasn't something I could make inside the report itself; it needed a change to the underlying data model or the way data was being loaded in the first place. I kept having to file that as a request for someone else and wait, and I realized I wanted to be the person who could actually make that fix. So I've been deliberately building the skills that sit upstream of where I was working before -- going deeper into SQL past basic querying, actually learning data modeling, understanding what it takes to build and maintain the pipeline that gets data into the model in the first place -- rather than just saying I want the title.
commonMistakes: Giving a vague answer about wanting to 'grow' without naming the actual difference between the two roles
Describing BI Engineering as just 'more advanced reporting' instead of upstream ownership (modeling, pipelines, reliability)
Stating interest without describing any concrete action already taken toward it
Not having a specific, real experience that motivated the shift
keyPoints: Names the real distinction: Analyst works within an existing model; BI Engineer owns the model/pipeline upstream of it
Motivation should come from a specific, real experience, not a vague sense of career progression
Shows concrete action already taken (specific skills being built), not just stated intention
Avoids treating BI Engineering as simply 'more advanced reporting'

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes the two roles
Gives a specific, credible motivation
Describes concrete action already taken

questions.title: Responding to a pull request sent back for changes
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time a teammate reviewed your work -- a query, a package, or a report -- and sent it back with specific changes requested. How did you respond?
questions.modelAnswer: This is a behavioral question testing professionalism and how a candidate handles feedback, not a request for a technical fact. A strong answer first frames code/report review correctly: it happens inside the Dev stage, before QA ever sees the change, as a normal second set of eyes on the approach -- not a personal judgment, and it's completely normal for a reviewer to send work back before it's allowed to merge. The answer should use the STAR structure (Situation, Task, Action, Result), with Action describing reading the specific feedback carefully, asking a clarifying question if the reasoning wasn't obvious rather than assuming or arguing, making the requested change (or explaining a respectful disagreement if there was a good reason), and re-requesting review. Result should state the concrete outcome -- the change was approved and merged, and ideally what was learned or changed going forward.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell one specific story rather than describe my attitude toward feedback in general. Situation: on my capstone's SSIS package, a reviewer flagged that my Lookup transformation had no error output configured, so a non-matching row would silently fail the whole package instead of being handled. Task: I needed to understand why that mattered and fix it properly, not just make the comment go away. Action: I asked the reviewer to walk me through what would actually happen with a non-matching row, since I hadn't considered it, then I configured the error output to redirect those rows to a dedicated log table instead of failing the package, and re-requested review with a short note explaining what I'd changed and why. Result: it was approved on the second pass, and I started checking every Lookup's error output by default on everything I built after that, which is the kind of habit a good review catches before it becomes a real production incident.
commonMistakes: Taking review feedback personally instead of treating it as a normal part of the Dev stage
Making the requested change without understanding why it was requested
Arguing defensively instead of asking a clarifying question when the reasoning isn't clear
Describing review feedback in general terms instead of telling one specific, real story with a stated Result
keyPoints: Code/report review happens inside the Dev stage, before QA -- it's a normal second set of eyes, not a personal judgment
Read specific feedback carefully; ask a clarifying question if the reasoning isn't obvious
Make the change (or explain a respectful disagreement), then re-request review
Use STAR and state the concrete Result -- what happened after the change was made

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Frames review feedback as a normal part of the process, not a personal setback
Tells a specific, real story using STAR
States a concrete Result
